Algeria scores high for power held by state-embedded actors (7.5 of 10) and middling for resilience (4.2). As a best estimate, outside influence would most likely come through Islamist political movements or through groups already close to the state's own institutions.
Algeria.imp: This map holds no evidence of hidden control in Algeria. With strong state bodies and limited outside checks, any such influence would be hard for citizens to see, so the openness of party funding and security appointments is the thing to watch.

The region was touched by the anticommunist web: in 1977 the Safari Club's member states flew Moroccan and Egyptian troops into neighbouring Zaire's Shaba province to back Mobutu. Power held by state-embedded actors scores high (8.0 of 10) and resilience middling (4.2), so as a best estimate any infiltration would most likely run through security and intelligence links or through foreign religious and diplomatic bodies already present.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has documented presence, and the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française (GLNF) are likely present but undocumented. Benin sits inside the region of the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern, in which presidents of Burkina Faso, Congo, Gabon, Guinea and Mali were reported to lead or oversee grand lodges. State-embedded actors score moderate (6.0 of 10) and resilience weak (3.8); as a best estimate, French-linked lodges are the most likely route.
Benin.imp: Nothing here shows a lodge or foreign body steering Benin's state. Given the pattern in nearby countries, the open question is whether senior officials belong to lodges that citizens are never told about.

Its conditions are among the more protective in the region: state-embedded actors score 4.5 of 10 and resilience 5.4. As a best estimate, any outside influence would more likely come through the regional networks recorded next door in South Africa, such as old British lodge and Rhodes-linked ties, than through a body already active inside the country.

Burkina Faso.d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that President Blaise Compaoré, who ruled from 1987 to 2014, was a former grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina. The same report said his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé, had succeeded him as grand master. That put the leadership of the country's main lodge first in the president's hands and then in his foreign minister's. These are press reports; no court or inquiry examined them. Burkina Faso is a head-of-state-and-minister case in the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern; the same 2012 article reported presidents leading or overseeing lodges in Guinea, Mali and Congo. The Order of Malta and the Gülen movement also have documented presence, and the Grand Orient de France and GLNF are likely present.
Burkina Faso.imp: For years the people running Burkina Faso's state also ran its main lodge, a private body whose membership and meetings the public could not see. Belonging to a lodge is lawful and no wrongdoing was found, but loyalties formed there were invisible to citizens. Watch whether ministers and presidents now disclose such memberships.

Burundi.imp: This map shows no hidden organisation inside Burundi's government. With power concentrated in the state and few checks, citizens would have little way to detect one if it existed.

Cabo Verde.d: This map documents no case for Cabo Verde. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the only organisation with documented presence. As a best estimate, any influence would most likely come through diplomatic and religious channels linked to Portugal and Europe.
Cabo Verde.imp: There is no sign here of hidden influence over Cabo Verde's government, and its institutions score as comparatively strong.

Cameroon.d: Le Monde reported in December 1999 that President Paul Biya gave tens of millions of francs between 1988 and 1992 to Raymond Bernard's Sovereign Order of the Initiatic Temple (OSTI) and CIRCES, including 40 million francs personally. The paper traced 11.2 million francs from the state oil company SNH to Bernard's personal account. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and would not comment on the payments. Bernard was questioned in the Solar Temple inquiry but not charged. OSTI is listed as headquartered in Cameroon, and Opus Dei, the Order of Malta and the Gülen movement also have documented presence. The case places Cameroon in two cross-border patterns: as members in government under 'faith movements placing members in the state', and as a head of state tied to an order under 'French lodges and African presidencies'.
Cameroon.imp: The reporting points to public oil money passing through the president to a private esoteric order, with no public accounting. Citizens learned of it only through a French newspaper years later, and no court ruled on it. Watch how the state oil company's spending is audited and who is allowed to see it.

Central African Republic.d: François Bozizé, president from 2003 to 2013, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting on African heads of state in lodges. A 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier said he joined under the sponsorship of Denis Sassou-Nguesso, president of neighbouring Congo, who is himself reported to be grand master of the Grand Lodge of Congo. Both items are press reports, not findings of a court or inquiry. The Central African Republic is a head-of-state case in the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern, and the Bozizé–Sassou link shows the pattern running between presidencies, not only from Paris. The Order of Malta has documented presence and the GLNF is likely present.
Central African Republic.imp: The reporting suggests a personal tie between two sitting presidents formed through a lodge, a channel citizens of either country could not see. It is reported, not proven. In a state that scores very weak on resilience (2.1 of 10), watch for private ties between leaders that shape decisions outside public view.

Chad.d: Idriss Déby, president from 1990 to 2021, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting and again in a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier; no lodge is named. In November 2017 a statement on the presidency's website said Déby had agreed to hand schools run by the Gülen movement to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation by 18 December 2017 and to expel people linked to the movement. Chad is a head-of-state case in the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern. In the 'faith movements placing members in the state' and 'exposure, purge and reversal' patterns it is a government that banned or purged the movement, one of several African states (with Guinea, Niger, Senegal, Somalia and Sudan) that handed Gülen schools to Maarif in 2017.
Chad.imp: Two outside forces show up in Chad's record: a lodge tie reported for the president, and a foreign government's state foundation taking over a rival movement's schools by presidential order. Families using those schools had no say in the transfer. Watch how foreign governments use their ties with Chad's presidency to settle their own disputes on Chadian soil.

Congo, Rep..d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Pascal Lissouba, president from 1992 to 1997, had been initiated at a Grand Orient de France lodge in Besançon. His successor and predecessor, Denis Sassou-Nguesso, is reported (Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique, 2013) to be grand master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Française. The 2013 dossier also said Sassou-Nguesso sponsored the initiation of François Bozizé, later president of the Central African Republic. These are press reports, not court or inquiry findings. Congo is a head-of-state case in the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern, with presidents tied to both main French obediences. The Order of Malta also has documented presence.
Congo, Rep..imp: Both men who held Congo's presidency in this record are reported to have ties to French-linked lodges, one of them as grand master. Citizens could not see what was agreed inside those lodges or with their French counterparts. Watch for lodge ties between presidents and foreign governments shaping decisions without public debate.

Cote d'Ivoire.d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Prime Minister Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio and Interior Minister Hamed Bakayoko were Freemasons, and that state prosecutor Simplice Koffi Kouadio had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire. The same report said President Alassane Ouattara was not officially known to be a member. These are press reports; no inquiry examined them. Côte d'Ivoire is a minister case in the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern, here reaching the head of government, the minister over police and a state prosecutor. Opus Dei and the Order of Malta also have documented presence, and the Grand Orient de France and GLNF are likely present.
Cote d'Ivoire.imp: The report puts the prime minister, the interior minister and a prosecutor in or near the same private body. Membership is lawful and nothing wrong was found, but citizens could not know whether people judging and policing them shared loyalties outside their offices. Watch whether prosecutors and security ministers disclose such ties.

Egypt.d: In 1976 General Kamal Hassan Ali, head of the Mukhabarat, signed the Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran. In 1977 France flew Egyptian and Moroccan troops into Zaire's Shaba province to back Mobutu, and Saudi Arabia paid Egypt $75 million for old Soviet weapons sent to Somalia's Siad Barre, as Mohamed Heikal documented from the Shah's seized archives. In June 2012 Mohamed Morsi, a senior Muslim Brotherhood figure, won the presidential election; the army removed him on 3 July 2013. A court banned the Brotherhood in September 2013, and on 25 December 2013 the interim cabinet declared it a terrorist organisation, two days after the Mansoura police bombing that Ansar Bait al-Maqdis claimed. In 2017 the Court of Cassation upheld Morsi's life sentence for leading an illegal group but threw out a 15-year term for stealing secret documents in the case alleging he passed secrets to Qatar, which Qatar denied. Egypt is a documented case in the anticommunist web (1945–1990), the case in 'movements that sought the state itself' where the movement won the presidency and was then banned as terrorist, and a banning government in 'exposure, purge and reversal'. Both the Brotherhood and the Safari Club are listed as headquartered here.
Egypt.imp: Egypt's record holds two different things. In the 1970s its intelligence chief joined a private pact of spy chiefs that moved troops and money across Africa without public debate. In 2012 a movement won the presidency openly, then was removed by the army, banned and its leader convicted. Watch for security agreements made outside parliament, and for whether terrorism labels are tested in open courts.

Gabon.d: Omar Bongo, initiated as a Freemason in 1953 and president from 28 November 1967 until his death on 8 June 2009, founded two Masonic bodies: the Grand Rite Equatorial, affiliated with the Grand Orient de France, and the Grand Lodge of Gabon, linked to the GLNF, and held the grand mastership until he died. In 2009 GLNF grand master François Stifani installed his son Ali Bongo as grand master of both; Ali Bongo became president the same year and kept the lodge post until after the August 2023 coup. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that ministers Paul Toungui and Séraphin Moundounga and National Security Council head Léon Paul Ngoulakia attended that 2009 installation, and that police chief Antoine Embinga, grand master of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon, was removed as head of police in January 2012. In October 2023 the Grand Lodge of Gabon replaced Ali Bongo with Jacques Denis Tsanga, governor of Haut-Ogooué and a former minister; transitional president Brice Oligui Nguema reportedly declined the post. These are press and book reports, not court findings. Gabon is the fullest case in the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern: the head of state held the grand mastership for more than 50 years, and a French grand master installed the president's son.
Gabon.imp: In Gabon the presidency and the leadership of the main lodges were held by the same family for decades, and a French lodge leader took part in passing the lodge post from father to son. Ministers, the security council head and the police chief sat in the same circles, out of public view. After the 2023 coup the lodge post moved to a governor, so watch whether the new rulers rebuild such ties.

By June 2017 Gülen-linked schools in Guinea had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry, as also happened in Niger, Sudan and Somalia. Liberia.d: William Tolbert, vice-president from 1952 to 1971 and president from 1971 to 1980, was grand master of the Masonic Order of Liberia. Lodge membership was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the ruling True Whig Party, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons. Tolbert was killed on 12 April 1980 in Samuel Doe's coup, along with much of the Masonic leadership. Doe then banned Freemasonry; he later lifted the ban, the order was formally reinstated in 1988, and Doe himself was initiated in 1989. Both cases come from histories of the Masonic Order of Liberia. Liberia is a head-of-state case in the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern and a ban-then-reversal case in 'exposure, purge and reversal'. The National Endowment for Democracy and the Order of Malta also have documented presence.
Liberia.imp: For decades the ruling party and the lodge were close to the same circle, so the people who chose Liberia's leaders met partly in private. The coup leader who banned the lodge joined it nine years later. Watch whether membership of private orders again becomes an unwritten condition for high office.

Nigeria.d: Nigeria's case is a legal barrier. Sections 66, 107, 137 and 182 of the 1999 Constitution disqualify members of secret societies from election to the National Assembly, state assemblies, the presidency and governorships; Section 38(4) bars anyone from belonging to one, and the Code of Conduct says a public officer may not belong to a society incompatible with the office. Commentators name the Ogboni fraternities, Freemasons and AMORC among the societies at issue. After the February 1999 election, runner-up Olu Falae petitioned that president-elect Olusegun Obasanjo was an Ogboni member and so disqualified; the election tribunal dismissed the petition, and the Reformed Ogboni Fraternity said it was non-political and not a secret society. Nigeria is the constitutional-ban case in the 'exposure, purge and reversal' pattern. Opus Dei, the Gülen movement and the Congress for Cultural Freedom have documented presence.
Nigeria.imp: Nigeria wrote into its constitution that secret-society members may not hold elected office, which shows how seriously the concern is taken. The one test of it against a president failed in the tribunal, so no official has been found in breach on this record. Watch how the rule is enforced and who decides which groups count as secret societies.

The Order of Malta also has documented presence, and the Grand Orient de France and GLNF are likely present.

The clearer outside reach is Turkey's: about 3,000 children's schools were closed at a foreign government's request. Senegal's institutions score fairly strong (resilience 5.9), so watch whether such foreign requests go through open, reviewable decisions.
