The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has documented presence and the United Grand Lodge of England is likely present but undocumented. Turkish government statements cited in Morocco's entry listed Sierra Leone among African states reported in June 2017 to have closed Gülen-linked schools. State-embedded actors score 8.0 of 10 and resilience 4.0; as a best estimate, English-rite lodge ties among officials are the most likely route.
Sierra Leone.imp: This map shows no hidden organisation in Sierra Leone's government. Watch whether officials disclose lodge memberships.

Somalia.d: By June 2017 Gülen-linked schools in Somalia had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry, as also happened in Guinea, Niger and Sudan. Somalia is a government that banned or purged the movement in the 'faith movements placing members in the state' and 'exposure, purge and reversal' patterns. The Muslim Brotherhood and the Order of Malta also have documented presence. Conditions are among the weakest on the map: state-embedded actors 8.0 of 10, resilience 1.9.
Somalia.imp: The one documented case shows a foreign government getting Somalia's government to hand it schools run by a movement it opposes. It says nothing about who controls the state itself. With very weak checks, watch which foreign governments gain this kind of access to Somali officials.

South Africa.d: Two networks reached inside South Africa's government on this record. A House of Commons committee censured Cecil Rhodes, Cape premier, over the 1895–96 Jameson Raid; Alfred Milner became High Commissioner in 1897; and from 1901 his young Oxford staff ('Milner's Kindergarten') held posts such as Transvaal Treasurer and Johannesburg town clerk and pressed for the 1910 Union. Those offices are on the record, while Carroll Quigley's claims that they formed Rhodes's secret society and caused the Boer War rest on him alone. One of them, Patrick Duncan, became Governor-General in 1937 and in 1939 refused Prime Minister Hertzog an election and asked Jan Smuts to form a government. From 1948 to 1994 every prime minister and state president, from D. F. Malan to F. W. de Klerk, belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret Afrikaner men's society founded in 1918, whose roughly 7,500 members were listed by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom in 1978. A 1979 report said all but two cabinet ministers were members, along with Defence Force chief Magnus Malan and 49 people in key posts at the SABC; security chief Hendrik van den Bergh had also been a member, and Broederbond chairman Gerrit Viljoen was made Administrator-General of South West Africa in 1979 and education minister in 1980. Smuts had ordered civil servants and teachers out of the Broederbond in the 1940s, but the order lapsed when Malan's party won in 1948. South Africa is the founding ground of the 'Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network', the case where the brotherhood ran the government in 'sworn brotherhoods that chose who governed', and a banning government in 'exposure, purge and reversal'.
South Africa.imp: For most of the 20th century, the people who led South Africa's state were also organised in private: first around Rhodes and Milner, then in a sworn society whose members were secret until journalists printed the list in 1978. Citizens could not see that the cabinet, the army command and the state broadcaster shared one hidden membership. The Broederbond link rests on published lists; the claims about Rhodes's secret society rest on one historian. Watch whether appointments to security, broadcasting and education posts can be traced to open processes.

South Sudan.d: This map documents no case for South Sudan. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta and the Atlas Network have documented presence. State-embedded actors score 9.0 of 10 and resilience 2.0. As a best estimate, influence would most likely come through armed factions, oil interests and the foreign governments that back them.
South Sudan.imp: No hidden organisation is shown here, but with almost no checks on the state, citizens could not tell who stands behind those in office.

Sudan.d: On 30 June 1989 Brigadier Omar al-Bashir seized power in a coup organised with Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, a movement derived from the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood. After Bashir fell in 2019, he and other military and Islamist figures were tried in Khartoum from 2020 for the coup, and Bashir admitted his role during the trial. In November 2019 the transitional government set up the Empowerment Removal Committee to remove people placed in state jobs under the 1989 regime; it dismissed judges, prosecutors and judicial staff, but on 7 October 2021 the High Court's appeals department overturned the dismissals and on 12 October ordered 15 staff back to work, a ruling the committee rejected. By June 2017 Gülen-linked schools had been handed to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation. Sudan is the case in 'movements that sought the state itself' where the movement won government by coup, and a purging government in 'exposure, purge and reversal', where the judicial purge was itself reversed by a court.
Sudan.imp: For 30 years, a political-religious movement that took power by coup placed its people throughout the state, including the courts. When a later government tried to remove them, a court reversed part of the purge, showing how hard such placements are to undo. Watch who controls appointments to judges and prosecutors after each change of power.

Tanzania.d: No case is documented for Tanzania on this map. Opus Dei and the Gülen movement have documented presence. State-embedded actors score 6.0 of 10 and resilience 4.2. As a best estimate, influence would most likely come through foreign governments pressing action against the Gülen movement, as several African states did in 2017, or through ties to the long-ruling party.
Tanzania.imp: This map shows no hidden organisation in Tanzania's government.

Togo.d: This map documents no case for Togo. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has documented presence; the Grand Orient de France and GLNF are likely present but undocumented, and Togo lies in the region of the 'French lodges and African presidencies' pattern. State-embedded actors score 7.5 of 10 and resilience 4.4. As a best estimate, French-linked lodges and ties around the presidency are the most likely routes.
Togo.imp: No case is shown here. Given the pattern in nearby French-speaking states, watch whether senior officials disclose lodge memberships.

Tunisia.d: After winning the October 2011 Constituent Assembly election, Ennahda led Tunisia's government: Hamadi Jebali was prime minister from December 2011 to March 2013 and Ali Laarayedh until January 2014, and Rafik Abdessalem, son-in-law of party leader Rached Ghannouchi, was foreign minister. Ennahda grew out of the Brotherhood tradition but says it has no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood. On 5 February 2025 a court sentenced Ghannouchi, speaker of parliament from 2019 to 2021, to a further 22 years for 'plotting against state security' in the Instalingo case; Abdessalem got 34 years and ex-prime minister Hichem Mechichi 35 years in absentia. Ghannouchi has been jailed since April 2023, received another 14 years in July 2025, and his party calls the case political. Tunisia is a 'won government' case in the 'movements that sought the state itself' pattern. Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Trilateral Commission also have documented presence.
Tunisia.imp: Ennahda came to power openly through an election, not in secret; the open question is how far a wider movement shaped it. Its leaders were later given long sentences in a case the party calls political. Watch whether such cases are heard in open courts with evidence the public can examine.

Uganda.d: No case is documented for Uganda on this map. Opus Dei, the Gülen movement, The Fellowship (The Family) and the Congress for Cultural Freedom have documented presence; the United Grand Lodge of England and Communion and Liberation are likely present but undocumented. State-embedded actors score 8.0 of 10 and resilience 3.7, and Uganda's reach score (4.18) is among the higher in Africa without a case. As a best estimate, the most likely route is through religious-political networks such as The Fellowship that build personal ties with leaders and legislators.
Uganda.imp: This map holds no documented case, but many outside networks are active and checks on the state are weak. Watch for foreign religious groups with direct access to leaders and lawmakers.

Zambia.d: This map documents no case for Zambia. The United Grand Lodge of England and the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) are likely present but undocumented. State-embedded actors score 6.5 of 10 and resilience 4.7. As a best estimate, influence would most likely come through English-rite lodge ties or through banking channels of the kind BCCI once ran.
Zambia.imp: No hidden organisation is shown in Zambia's government on this map.

Zimbabwe.d: No case is documented for Zimbabwe on this map. The United Grand Lodge of England, BCCI and the Rhodes Trust are likely present but undocumented, and the 'Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network' recorded in South Africa touches the region. State-embedded actors score 8.0 of 10 and resilience 3.0. As a best estimate, influence would most likely come through the ruling party and security forces, or through financial networks linked to them.
Zimbabwe.imp: This map shows no hidden organisation in Zimbabwe's government. With weak checks, influence around the ruling party and army would be hard for citizens to see.

Afghanistan.d: No case is documented on this map for Afghanistan. The only tracked organisation with documented presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; the Gülen movement, the Iran-based Hojjatieh Society and the Asia Foundation are likely present but undocumented. Conditions are among the weakest in the region: state-embedded actors score 9 out of 10 and resilience 1.5. As a best-judgement estimate, outside reach would most likely come through neighbouring states' religious networks, such as Hojjatieh from Iran, or through Turkey's campaign against Gülen-linked schools that the map records across Central Asia.
Afghanistan.imp: With almost no checks on those who hold power, any infiltration would be hard for citizens to see or challenge. The empty record reflects missing evidence, not proof that nothing happened.

Armenia.d: This map holds no documented case for Armenia. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has documented presence, and the Russian state's Russkiy Mir Foundation is likely present but undocumented. State-embedded actors score fairly low (3.5 of 10) and resilience sits in the middle (5.6). As an estimate, the most likely source of outside reach is Russian state-backed cultural and diaspora networks such as Russkiy Mir.
Armenia.imp: Nothing here shows a captured office. What to watch is whether foreign-funded cultural bodies begin sponsoring politicians or parties.

Azerbaijan.d: Azerbaijan's one documented case is the state moving against a foreign movement. On 18 June 2014 Gülen-linked schools in the country (11 high schools, 13 university-entrance preparation centres and a private university) were taken over by the Azerbaijan International Education Company, in which the state oil company SOCAR holds shares. The company gave financial viability as the reason; the takeover followed requests from Turkish Prime Minister Erdogan for help against the Gülen movement. On the map's patterns, Azerbaijan sits in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal' as a government that banned or purged the organisation. The Grey Wolves also have documented presence, and the World Economic Forum is likely present.
Azerbaijan.imp: The record shows a state oil company carrying out another government's request against a religious school network. Families using those schools had no say in the transfer. Watch for state companies used as tools in disputes between governments.

Bahrain.d: Bahrain's Interior Ministry obtained an Interpol Red Notice for Hakeem al-Araibi, a footballer and dissident who had fled the country in 2014 and was a refugee in Australia. Thai police arrested him on arrival in Bangkok in November 2018. Interpol withdrew the notice days later because its 2015 policy bars notices sought by the country a refugee fled; Thailand still held extradition proceedings until prosecutors dropped the case on 11 February 2019. This places Bahrain in the pattern 'Governments and industries inside international bodies' as the government involved. The Muslim Brotherhood also has documented presence.
Bahrain.imp: This case is a government using an international police channel to reach someone who had escaped it, not an outside group reaching into Bahrain. Interpol's own rules stopped it, but only after he had been jailed abroad. Watch for wanted notices aimed at exiles and critics.

Bangladesh.d: In January 2012 the Bangladesh army announced it had stopped a coup attempt by serving and retired officers it described as religious extremists, and named Hizb ut-Tahrir, banned in the country since 2009, among those behind it. Two retired officers were arrested and a serving major was named as a fugitive. The finding is the army's own press briefing. The map counts Bangladesh in 'Movements that sought the state itself' as a country where the group tried to take the army, the same role Pakistan holds after its 2012 court-martial of a brigadier. BCCI is likely present but undocumented.
Bangladesh.imp: A banned movement had reached officers inside the army, the body able to remove a government. What the public knows comes from the army itself, with no trial record in this file. Watch for recruitment inside the security forces by groups that reject elections.

Bhutan.d: No case is documented on this map for Bhutan, and no tracked organisation has documented or likely presence. State-embedded actors score low (3 of 10) and resilience sits just below the middle (4.7). As an estimate, any outside reach would most likely come through its two large neighbours, India and China, which host networks on this map: the RSS in India and the United Front Work Department in China.
Bhutan.imp: The record is empty, which may mean little activity or little reporting. Political groups tied to neighbouring states would be the thing to watch.

Brunei.d: This map records no case and no tracked organisation for Brunei. State-embedded actors score low (3 of 10) and resilience sits just below the middle (4.6). As a best guess, outside reach would come through religious movements recorded in neighbouring Malaysia and Indonesia, such as Hizb ut-Tahrir, which Indonesia banned in 2017.
Brunei.imp: Nothing has been documented. An empty record can mean little activity or little public reporting.

Cambodia.d: No case is documented on this map for Cambodia. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has documented presence; the Gülen movement and China's United Front Work Department are likely present but undocumented. State-embedded actors score very high (9 of 10) and resilience low (3.5). As an estimate, the most likely route in is Chinese state influence through the United Front, which the map documents in Taiwan and Australia; one Australian case ran through a federation of Chinese organisations for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.
Cambodia.imp: Where people inside the state already serve their own interests, a foreign state can work through them without leaving a public trace. Watch for business deals and community bodies that bring officials and foreign agencies together.

China.d: China appears on this map mostly as a state that reaches outward and works through international bodies. Meng Hongwei, a Vice-Minister of Public Security, was elected Interpol's first Chinese president on 10 November 2016; he disappeared after flying to China on 25 September 2018, the Communist Party's discipline commission announced an investigation on 7 October, and in January 2020 a Tianjin court sentenced him to 13 and a half years for taking more than 14.5 million yuan in bribes, a case his wife, granted asylum in France, calls political. While he was president, in February 2018, Interpol removed China's Red Notice for Dolkun Isa, a World Uyghur Congress leader living in Germany, and China protested; rights groups record 1,546 detentions or deportations of Uyghurs from 28 countries since 1997. In December 2019 China sanctioned the US National Endowment for Democracy after its Foreign Ministry called NED an intelligence front and listed 20 years of its grants to Hong Kong groups, which is the government's assertion, not an independent finding. On the patterns, China is the sponsoring state in 'One state's networks inside another' through the United Front Work Department, headquartered here, whose cases the map records in Taiwan and Australia. It is the government involved in 'Governments and industries inside international bodies', the place the money went in 'Intelligence money behind international NGOs', and a purging government in 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
China.imp: The record shows a ruling party that placed its own security official at the head of the world police body, then removed him through its own discipline system, while treating foreign-funded groups as hostile. Chinese citizens could not see the evidence behind his disappearance and trial. Watch for wanted notices against exiles and for overseas community bodies tied to the United Front.

Cyprus.d: No case is documented on this map for Cyprus. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta and the Trilateral Commission have documented presence; the United Grand Lodge of England and Turkey's Grey Wolves are likely present but undocumented. State-embedded actors (4 of 10) and resilience (4.5) both sit near the middle. As an estimate, the most likely outside reach is from Turkish nationalist networks such as the Grey Wolves, whose use by Turkish state bodies a 1997 Turkish parliamentary inquiry confirmed.
Cyprus.imp: No office is shown to be captured. The thing to watch is nationalist groups from a neighbouring state acting through local followers.

Georgia.d: This map documents no case for Georgia. The Grand Orient de France, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta and the Gülen movement have documented presence, and the Atlas Network is likely present. State-embedded actors and resilience both sit near the middle (4 and 5 of 10). As a best judgement, the most likely pressure points are Turkey's campaign against Gülen-linked schools, which the map records across Central Asia, and pro-market think tanks of the Atlas kind seeking policy roles.
Georgia.imp: Presence of these groups is lawful and not misconduct. Watch for a foreign government asking Georgia to hand over teachers or close schools, as happened in Kyrgyzstan and Malaysia.

India.d: India's two documented cases are about a century apart. Carroll Quigley writes that Lionel Curtis formed a study group inside the London Round Table about 1911, joined by three India Office officials (Sir William Duke, Malcolm Seton and Sir Lionel Abrahams), which settled on 'dyarchy': handing some provincial functions to elected Indian ministers. Lord Chelmsford told the Lords in November 1927 that he had been handed a pamphlet on the principle at the India Office in 1916, thinking it came from an official committee, and dyarchy was enacted in the Government of India Act 1919. This rests on Quigley's history and Curtis's own 1920 book, not a court or inquiry, and is India's entry in the 'Rhodes, Milner and the Round Table network' pattern. The second case is Narendra Modi, who joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh as a boy, was a full-time organiser (pracharak) from the early 1970s, was seconded to the BJP in 1985 and became prime minister in 2014; his official biographies set this out and the RSS has acknowledged it. That places India in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' with members in government; the RSS, headquartered in India, is also documented in Nepal and Australia.
India.imp: In 1919 a plan drafted by a private study group became the shape of India's provincial government, and the viceroy who received it thought it was official. Today the head of government came up through an organisation that publishes no membership rolls, so citizens cannot see how many other officials share that path. RSS membership is lawful; what to watch is whether decisions are settled inside the organisation before they reach public bodies.

Indonesia.d: In the late 1950s the Ford Foundation paid for University of Indonesia economists to take graduate degrees at the University of California, Berkeley. After Suharto took power in 1966 they became his economic team: Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency BAPPENAS from 1967 to 1983 and wrote the Five-Year Development Plans, Ali Wardhana was Finance Minister from June 1968 to March 1983, and Emil Salim and Mohammad Sadli also held ministries. Their 1966 programme, first presented to Suharto at the army staff college in August 1966, cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened the country to foreign investors. John Perkins says that in the 1970s he inflated growth forecasts for the engineering firm Chas. T. Main so that Indonesia would take large loans; a 2006 New York Times check found no evidence for his larger claims, and the US State Department called much of his book a fabrication. Together these place Indonesia in 'Lenders, aid programmes and trained technocrats' as a country whose economy was run by the trainees. Separately, in July 2017 the government revoked Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia's legal status, warned that civil-servant members would be dismissed, and saw the ban upheld by the courts in 2018, which puts Indonesia in 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Indonesia.imp: For 16 years the people writing Indonesia's plans and budgets had been trained through one foreign foundation's programme, and their programme was set before they took office. Perkins's loan claims remain his own and unproven. Watch where economic ministers were trained and who paid for it, and whether bans on groups are applied to civil servants with due process.

Iran.d: General Nematollah Nassiri, head of the Shah's intelligence service SAVAK, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco; the documents were found in the Shah's archives after the 1979 revolution, and Saudi Prince Turki al-Faisal confirmed the club in 2002. This is Iran's entry in 'The anticommunist web, 1945–1990', alongside Saudi intelligence chief Kamal Adham. Jafar Sharif-Emami, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Iran for several years, was the Shah's prime minister in 1960–61 and again from 27 August to early November 1978, according to biographical accounts rather than any official finding. After the revolution, Ayatollah Khomeini attacked the Hojjatieh Society in a speech on 12 July 1983; its founder Mahmoud Halabi suspended it the same day and its affiliates were purged from decision-making, academic and educational bodies. Former members are reported to have later held posts in the judiciary and security system, but claims about senior figures and about influence under President Ahmadinejad are contested. Hojjatieh is headquartered in Iran and places the country in 'Faith movements placing members in the state'.
Iran.imp: Before 1979 Iran's intelligence chief was in a secret pact with foreign spy services and a lodge Grand Master led the government in its last months, and citizens had no way to know either. After 1979 the contest moved inside the religious state, where one society was purged but is reported to have kept members in office. Claims about who belongs today are disputed and should be read with that in mind.

Iraq.d: No case is documented on this map for Iraq. The Muslim Brotherhood, Hizb ut-Tahrir and BCCI have documented presence; the Gülen movement and the Iran-based Hojjatieh Society are likely present but undocumented. State-embedded actors score high (8.5 of 10) and resilience low (3.3). As a best-judgement estimate, infiltration would most likely come through religious and political networks tied to Iran and Turkey, and from movements such as Hizb ut-Tahrir, which the map records recruiting army officers in Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Iraq.imp: With insiders already strong and checks weak, foreign-linked groups could gain posts with little public record. The empty case list reflects missing documentation, not proof of absence.

Israel.d: This map documents no case for Israel. Organisations with documented presence are the Legion of Christ, the Unification Church, the Trilateral Commission and the Congress for Cultural Freedom; the Church of Scientology and the World Economic Forum are likely present. State-embedded actors and resilience both score 5.5 of 10. As an estimate, the most likely route of influence is elite forums such as the Trilateral Commission and the WEF, where officials meet business leaders, rather than religious movements.
Israel.imp: Taking part in a forum is lawful and not evidence of control. Watch for policy that takes shape inside private forums before it reaches the public.

Japan.d: Most of Japan's record runs through the Unification Church and the governing LDP. In 1968 former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi, Shinzo Abe's grandfather, founded the International Federation for Victory over Communism with Ryoichi Sasakawa and Yoshio Kodama to handle the church's political operations, and a 1975 FBI report named Kishi and Sasakawa as heads of its Japanese branch. After Abe was shot dead on 8 July 2022 by Tetsuya Yamagami, who blamed the church for his family's ruin, the LDP's own survey of 8 September 2022 found 179 of its 379 Diet members reporting church ties and 17 using followers as campaign volunteers, among them Defense Minister Nobuo Kishi, Abe's younger brother, and former economy minister Koichi Hagiuda; economic revitalization minister Daishiro Yamagiwa resigned over his ties on 24 October 2022. In March 2025 the Tokyo District Court ordered the church dissolved, finding 1,559 victims of unlawful donation solicitation and about 20.4 billion yen taken over roughly 40 years; the Tokyo High Court upheld the order on 4 March 2026, and Yamagami was sentenced to life on 21 January 2026. Other faith-linked groups sat close to the cabinet too: press and research counts put 15 of 19 ministers in Abe's September 2014 cabinet in Nippon Kaigi and 16 of 19 in Shinto Seiji Renmei's Diet league, and Soka Gakkai's party Komeito was an LDP coalition partner from 1999 until it left on 10 October 2025. In 1995 a US Senate staff report listed three former Self-Defense Force members in Aum Shinrikyo, and a Tokyo police officer who followed Aum confessed to a role in shooting the National Police Agency chief, though prosecutors twice declined to charge him. Japan is the heaviest entry in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' and appears in 'Exposure, purge and reversal' through the Senate inquiry and the court dissolution order.
Japan.imp: For decades a church that courts later found had taken money unlawfully from 1,559 people worked alongside ruling-party politicians, from a former prime minister founding its political arm to campaign volunteers in the 2020s, and the public learned the scale only after an assassination. Membership in Nippon Kaigi, Shinto Seiji Renmei or Soka Gakkai is lawful and the cabinet counts are reported, not ruled on, but they show how many ministers shared ties to the same few groups. The party survey relied on lawmakers reporting on themselves, so watch whether disclosure continues.

Jordan.d: On 23 April 2025 Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya banned all activities of the Muslim Brotherhood and said its assets would be seized. The ban followed the arrest of 16 people, including Brotherhood members, over an alleged plot involving weapons; the group denied knowledge of it. The Brotherhood's political arm, the Islamic Action Front, had won 31 of 138 seats in the September 2024 election, making it the largest party in parliament. The map lists Jordan as a government that banned the group in 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal', a step Saudi Arabia and the UAE took in 2014. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, Hizb ut-Tahrir and Chas. T. Main also have documented presence, and Le Cercle is likely present.
Jordan.imp: Here the movement reached parliament openly through elections, and the government then banned the organisation behind the largest party. The weapons plot is the government's account; this file holds no court finding on it. Watch what happens to the party's elected seats.

Kazakhstan.d: After Turkey's July 2016 coup attempt, Ankara asked Central Asian governments to close Gülen-linked schools, and Kazakhstan declined. On 18 October 2016 the sponsoring foundation KATEV announced that its 33 Turkish-Kazakh lyceums, co-founded by the Gülen movement, would be renamed 'Bilim' Innovative Lyceums; RFE/RL reported no Kazakh government order behind the change. The map places Kazakhstan in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' through this schools sector. Opus Dei, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Grey Wolves also have documented presence; the WEF, Russia's Russkiy Mir Foundation and Interpol are likely present.
Kazakhstan.imp: Unlike Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan kept the schools open and they renamed themselves. The record shows a foreign government pressing for closures, not Gülen members found in Kazakh offices. Watch for Turkish requests over teachers or wanted notices, which elsewhere in the region led to removals.

Korea, DPR.d: No case is documented on this map for North Korea. The Unification Church is the only tracked organisation with documented presence. Conditions are the most extreme in this file: state-embedded actors score 10 of 10 and resilience 1.6. As a best-judgement estimate, any outside reach would happen only on terms the state itself sets, through contacts such as the Unification Church's, rather than through hidden placements in office.
Korea, DPR.imp: With power held almost wholly by the state and no independent checks, outsiders cannot place people without the leadership's consent, and citizens cannot see any dealings. Records are unlikely to emerge.

Korea, Rep..d: The Unification Church, headquartered in South Korea, is behind four of its five cases. In 1978 the US House Fraser subcommittee found that the Moon Organization had influential allies in the Seoul government, naming KCIA founder Kim Jong-pil and Pak Chon-kyu; that a Moon business was an important defence contractor making M-16 rifles; and that in late 1977 Moon representatives acted in ways suggesting they were secret envoys of the Korean government. In 2026 three convictions followed a special counsel's case: on 28 January the Seoul Central District Court jailed former first lady Kim Keon-hee for one year and eight months for receiving a Chanel bag worth 12 million won and a Graff necklace worth 62 million won from the church in July 2022 (she was acquitted on other charges); on 16 July the Supreme Court upheld two years for former PPP floor leader Kweon Seong-dong, who took 100 million won from church official Yun Young-ho in January 2022, and he lost his seat; and on 31 August church leader Han Hak-ja got two years, the court finding that the church used its money to expand political influence around the presidential election (the church said it would appeal). Separately, a joint prosecutor-police team found at least 56,472 Shincheonji members registered as People Power Party members between July 2021 and August 2023, and on 13 July 2026 founder Lee Man-hee and seven other leaders were indicted under the Political Parties Act. These place South Korea in 'Faith movements placing members in the state'. Through the 1970s KCIA and Tongsun Park payments to US congressmen ('Koreagate') it is also the sponsoring state in 'One state's networks inside another', and the Fraser inquiry puts it in 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Korea, Rep..imp: Courts have now found that a church paid the president's wife and a ruling-party leader around the 2022 presidential election, and prosecutors say a second church registered tens of thousands of members in the governing party in the same period; the Shincheonji case is an indictment, not a verdict. Voters at the time could see neither. In the 1970s the same church had worked alongside Seoul's intelligence service abroad. Watch party membership drives and gifts to the president's household.

Kuwait.d: After the 1990 Iraqi invasion, Kuwait's Muslim Brotherhood broke with the international Brotherhood and founded the Islamic Constitutional Movement (Hadas). Hadas regularly won several seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and occasionally sent members to the cabinet. A coalition including Hadas was out of parliament after boycotting the 2013 elections. On the map Kuwait is the case in 'Movements that sought the state itself' where the movement won a share of government through elections. The Trilateral Commission also has documented presence.
Kuwait.imp: This was open participation, not a hidden placement: voters chose Hadas candidates knowing where the party came from. Kuwait differs from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which listed the Brotherhood as terrorist. Watch whether such parties stay inside elections or are pushed out of them.

Kyrgyzstan.d: Orhan Inandi, president of the Sapat network of Turkish-founded schools and a Kyrgyz citizen, disappeared in Bishkek in mid-2021. On 5 July 2021 President Erdogan said on TRT Haber that Inandi, whom he called a FETO leader, had been 'captured and taken to Turkey'. In August 2021 Kyrgyzstan's Military Prosecutor's Office opened proceedings for negligence and breach of border-service rules against border officers of the State Committee for National Security who let him be taken out of the country. The map places Kyrgyzstan in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' and, for this inquiry, in 'Exposure, purge and reversal'. Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Grey Wolves are likely present but undocumented.
Kyrgyzstan.imp: The reach here was by a foreign government into Kyrgyz security, which allowed a citizen to be removed from the country. The Kyrgyz case concerns the officers' negligence; this file holds no finding on anything more. Watch for border and security officers acting for another state.

Laos.d: This map records no case for Laos and no tracked organisation with documented or likely presence. State-embedded actors score fairly high (7.5 of 10) and resilience low (3.4). As a best-judgement estimate, outside influence would most likely come from China's United Front work, which the map documents in Taiwan and Australia; the Australian conviction of Di Sanh Duong involved a federation of Chinese organisations for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.
Laos.imp: Weak checks mean such influence would leave little public trace. The absence of cases is a gap in evidence, not a clean record.

Lebanon.d: No case is documented on this map for Lebanon, though it is listed as the headquarters of Hizb ut-Tahrir, which places it in 'Movements that sought the state itself'. Opus Dei, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the Muslim Brotherhood and the Trilateral Commission also have documented presence, and the Grand Orient de France is likely present. State-embedded actors score very high (9.5 of 10) and resilience low (3.1). As an estimate, infiltration would most likely come from religious and political movements tied to outside states, including the kind of officer recruitment Hizb ut-Tahrir attempted in Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Lebanon.imp: The group headquartered here has elsewhere tried to recruit army officers for a coup. With insiders already powerful, foreign-linked factions could hold office without records. The security forces are the place to watch.

Malaysia.d: In May 2017 Malaysian police arrested Turgay Karaman and Ihsan Aslan, and two days later academic Ismet Ozcelik, under a security law allowing 28 days' detention without trial. They were deported to Turkey on the night of 11 May 2017; police chief Khalid Abu Bakar said Ankara had cancelled their travel documents, so they were treated as illegal immigrants. Turkey accused them of Gülen ('FETO') links, and Human Rights Watch condemned the deportations. The map places Malaysia among governments that banned or purged the organisation in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'. Opus Dei also has documented presence; the United Grand Lodge of England, Hizb ut-Tahrir, Soka Gakkai, Nugan Hand Bank, the Atlas Network and the United Front Work Department are likely present.
Malaysia.imp: The record shows Malaysian police acting on another government's request, using detention without trial. The three men had no court hearing in Malaysia in this record. Watch for foreign governments cancelling passports to get critics sent back.

Maldives.d: No case is documented on this map for the Maldives, and no tracked organisation has documented or likely presence. State-embedded actors score near the middle (5.5 of 10) and resilience a little below it (4.0). As an estimate, outside influence would most likely come through networks based in India or through Gulf-backed religious movements of the kind recorded elsewhere in this file.
Maldives.imp: The empty record may reflect little reporting. Foreign-funded religious or political groups would be the thing to watch.

Mongolia.d: On 27 July 2018 Veysel Akcay, general manager of the Empathy Worldwide Educational Institution, which ran Gülen-linked Turkish-Mongolian schools, was seized in Ulaanbaatar. Mongolian authorities temporarily grounded a plane at the airport and he was released the same day. Turkish Minute and the Stockholm Center for Freedom reported that Turkey's MIT intelligence service carried out the abduction; Mongolian authorities said they had no specific knowledge of an abduction and were investigating. The map places Mongolia in 'Faith movements placing members in the state', in the same run of actions against Gülen-linked school staff seen in Kyrgyzstan and Malaysia. The Unification Church is likely present but undocumented.
Mongolia.imp: Mongolian officials stopped the removal, unlike Kyrgyz border officers three years later. Who carried out the seizure rests on press reports, not a finding. Watch for foreign intelligence services acting on a country's soil against its residents.

Myanmar.d: No case is documented on this map for Myanmar. The only tracked organisation with documented presence is the Congress for Cultural Freedom. State-embedded actors score 9 of 10 and resilience 1.5, among the weakest in the region. As a best-judgement estimate, outside reach would most likely come from China's state networks, given the United Front cases the map records in Taiwan and Australia.
Myanmar.imp: Where power sits with insiders and checks are absent, foreign influence passes through those insiders rather than into visible offices. The public would see little of it.

Nepal.d: This map documents no case for Nepal. The Unification Church and India's Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh have documented presence; the Atlas Network is likely present. State-embedded actors score high (8 of 10) and resilience low (3.9). As an estimate, the most likely outside reach is from India through the RSS, the movement whose former full-time organiser Narendra Modi became India's prime minister in 2014.
Nepal.imp: A neighbouring country's governing movement is present here. Watch for its affiliates backing Nepali parties or candidates.

Oman.d: No case is documented on this map for Oman, and no tracked organisation has documented presence; BCCI and Le Cercle are listed as likely present. State-embedded actors (4.5 of 10) and resilience (5.3) are both near the middle. As an estimate, the most likely route of outside influence is private finance and elite networks of the kind BCCI ran with Abu Dhabi and Saudi figures.
Oman.imp: Nothing has been shown. BCCI's record in the Gulf suggests watching who owns, and who sits on the boards of, banks close to the state.

Pakistan.d: Brigadier Ali Khan of army general headquarters was arrested in May 2011, and in August 2012 a military court convicted him and four majors of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, which is banned in Pakistan; he was sentenced to five years. The army said the group had tried to recruit officers to its programme of a coup and a caliphate. This makes Pakistan, like Bangladesh the same year, a country in 'Movements that sought the state itself' where the group tried to take the army. Separately, on 28 December 2018 a three-judge Supreme Court bench headed by Chief Justice Mian Saqib Nisar ordered the government to ban the Gülen movement and the Pak-Turk International Cag Education Foundation and to hand its schools to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation, saying Pakistan was bound by an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation declaration. That places Pakistan among governments that banned the group in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'. BCCI also has documented presence; the Atlas Network and the Asia Foundation are likely present.
Pakistan.imp: A banned movement had reached a brigadier at army headquarters, close to where coups are decided. In a separate line, Pakistan's top court handed a school network to a foreign state's foundation. Watch for recruitment inside the officer corps, and for foreign governments' demands carried out through domestic courts.

Philippines.d: Iglesia ni Cristo, headquartered in the Philippines with about 2.6 million members in the 2015 census, votes as a bloc it calls the 'Unity Vote'; it backed Benigno Aquino III in 2010, Rodrigo Duterte in 2016 and, on 3 May 2022, Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Sara Duterte and 12 Senate candidates. From 27 to 31 August 2015 its members protested at the Department of Justice and occupied parts of EDSA after Justice Secretary Leila de Lima acted on a complaint by a minister the church had expelled; police put the peak crowd at about 15,400, and Vice-President Jejomar Binay backed the protest. Duterte later appointed the church's executive minister, Eduardo Manalo, as Special Envoy of the President for Overseas Filipinos' Concerns, with papers dated 13 February 2018. On 30 June 2026 the church held a rally of about 12,000 on EDSA for Senator Rodante Marcoleta, a member elected in 2025 with its support, who was set to be charged by the Ombudsman for failing to declare 75 million pesos in campaign contributions. Apollo Quiboloy, founder of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ, was described by Duterte as his spiritual adviser and lent him his jet in the 2016 campaign; a US grand jury indicted him in 2021, and Philippine police arrested him in September 2024 on child-abuse and trafficking charges. All five cases place the Philippines in 'Faith movements placing members in the state'.
Philippines.imp: A church that delivers votes as a bloc has seen its leader given an official post by a president it endorsed, has massed crowds against a justice secretary's probe, and now rallies for a member-senator facing a charge. Citizens cannot see what, if anything, is agreed in exchange for an endorsement. The Quiboloy case is at the charge stage, with no verdict. Watch whom the bloc endorses and what posts or protection follow.

Qatar.d: No case is documented on this map for Qatar, and no tracked organisation has documented presence; the Muslim Brotherhood and Interpol are listed as likely present. State-embedded actors score 6.5 of 10 and resilience 5.5. As an estimate, the most likely concerns are ties to the Muslim Brotherhood (Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain withdrew their ambassadors from Qatar a day before Saudi Arabia listed the Brotherhood as terrorist in March 2014) and the use of international bodies of the kind the UAE pursued at Interpol.
Qatar.imp: Nothing is documented inside Qatar's government. Watch how disputes between Gulf governments play out through banned-group lists and international police channels.

Saudi Arabia.d: Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence from 1965 until his dismissal on 19 January 1979, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Egypt, Morocco and Iran, and his later successor Prince Turki al-Faisal confirmed the club publicly in 2002. Adham was also a major BCCI shareholder; US prosecutors said he played a key role in the bank's secret and illegal takeover of First American bank in Washington, and under a plea agreement he paid a $105 million fine and was barred from the finance sector. Those two cases put Saudi Arabia in 'The anticommunist web, 1945–1990' and 'Banks that carried the hidden money'. From 1974 the US-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation, co-chaired by the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi finance minister, ran 16 formal projects that a March 1979 US General Accounting Office report found were funded almost entirely from a Saudi trust account in the US Treasury, recycling petrodollars into US goods and services; John Perkins's claim that Chas. T. Main worked on Saudi projects then is his own. That places the kingdom in 'Lenders, aid programmes and trained technocrats'. On 7 March 2014 the government listed the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist, without naming any Saudi officials, which counts in 'Movements that sought the state itself' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Saudi Arabia.imp: One man ran the kingdom's intelligence service, joined a secret pact of spy chiefs and held a large stake in a bank that broke US law, and the public learned of it only years later. The economic commission shows Saudi money paying for US advisers working with its own ministries. Watch for intelligence and security officials holding private financial stakes.

Singapore.d: No case is documented on this map for Singapore. Opus Dei, Shincheonji and BCCI have documented presence; the United Grand Lodge of England, Soka Gakkai, Nugan Hand Bank, the Trilateral Commission and China's United Front Work Department are listed as likely present. State-embedded actors score very low (1.5 of 10) and resilience high (7.8). As a best-judgement estimate, the most likely routes are United Front work through Chinese community associations, as documented in Australia, and the use of the city's banks to move money, as BCCI and Nugan Hand did elsewhere.
Singapore.imp: Strong institutions make hidden placements harder, but a financial centre attracts money that needs hiding. Watch community associations that link donors to politicians.

Sri Lanka.d: Ranil Wickremesinghe, who served several times as prime minister and was president from July 2022 to 2024, is named among current political figures who are members of the Mont Pelerin Society. His membership and his offices are documented; no forum has found that the society directed his decisions. The map places Sri Lanka in 'Private forums where officials meet money' with a member placed in office, the same role New Zealand holds through former finance minister Ruth Richardson. Opus Dei and the Atlas Network also have documented presence; the United Grand Lodge of England and Aum Shinrikyo are likely present.
Sri Lanka.imp: This is lawful membership, not a found wrong. It tells readers which policy circle a head of state belonged to; watch whether economic reforms follow that circle's programmes.

Syria.d: No case is documented on this map for Syria. The Muslim Brotherhood, Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Grey Wolves have documented presence. State-embedded actors score 10 of 10 and resilience 2.0. As an estimate, infiltration would most likely come through armed and political movements tied to neighbouring states, including Turkish nationalist networks, and through movements that seek to take the state itself.
Syria.imp: Where insiders hold nearly all power and checks are missing, foreign-linked groups can act without any public record. The lack of cases reflects a lack of evidence.

Taiwan.d: Taiwan is the main target in this region of 'One state's networks inside another', with the Chinese state as sponsor. In August 2018 Taipei prosecutors raided the Chinese Unity Promotion Party and its founder Chang An-le, a former Bamboo Union gang leader, under the National Security, Political Donations and Organized Crime Prevention Acts; Chang said the party's money from China came from his company's profits there. Courts have since convicted: Gong He Party chairman Chou Ke-chi got two years in June 2025 for taking Fujian money for the party's 2022 campaigns; Lin Hsueh-feng got four years on 28 May 2025 for taking Chiayi village and ward chiefs on trips paid by a Chinese city's Taiwan Affairs Office, where officials urged them to vote for a particular party's candidate; and on 25 September 2025 four former DPP members, including an assistant to Foreign Minister Joseph Wu and a Presidential Office consultant, were jailed for spying for China's Central Military Commission, passing on William Lai's travel schedules. Indictments are pending against former legislator and Mainland Affairs Council deputy head Chang Hsien-yao, accused of taking instructions to promote Terry Gou's 2024 presidential bid and meeting Wang Huning in Beijing, and against two people accused of routing Jiangsu money to a 2022 New Taipei council candidate. All the sentences can be appealed. Taiwan is also listed as headquarters of the World Anti-Communist League in 'The anticommunist web, 1945–1990'.
Taiwan.imp: Courts have found Chinese money behind small parties and local officials' trips, and Chinese military intelligence recruits inside the offices of the president and the foreign minister. Voters in local races could not see who paid for campaigns or trips. Several cases are still at indictment or open to appeal. Watch the funding of small parties, paid trips across the strait, and staff with access to leaders' schedules.

Tajikistan.d: In May 2015 President Emomali Rahmon issued a decree overruling a 1994 cabinet decision that had let Gülen-linked Turkish schools operate, closing seven of them from September 2015. The schools, under investigation since January 2015, were transferred to the state and rebranded as schools for gifted children. The map places Tajikistan among governments that banned or purged the movement in 'Faith movements placing members in the state' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta also has documented presence; Hizb ut-Tahrir and Interpol are likely present.
Tajikistan.imp: The president closed a foreign-linked school network by decree, and this file holds no court ruling on it. Watch whether such decrees extend to teachers and families, and whether Interpol channels are used against them.

Thailand.d: No case is documented against Thailand's own government on this map, though Thai police appear in Bahrain's case: they arrested refugee footballer Hakeem al-Araibi in Bangkok in November 2018 on a Bahraini Red Notice, and prosecutors dropped the extradition on 11 February 2019. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the Unification Church and the World Anti-Communist League have documented presence; Nugan Hand Bank, China's United Front Work Department and the Asia Foundation are likely present. State-embedded actors score 7 of 10 and resilience 5. As an estimate, the most likely outside reach is through foreign governments' police requests and Chinese United Front work.
Thailand.imp: Thai police have acted on another state's wanted notice against a refugee. Watch which foreign requests they act on, and whether exiles are held.

Timor-Leste.d: This map documents no case for Timor-Leste. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta and Aginter Press have documented presence. State-embedded actors score 4.5 of 10 and resilience 3.9. As an estimate, outside influence would most likely come through its larger neighbours, Indonesia and Australia, both of which have documented cases on this map.
Timor-Leste.imp: A state with weak checks is open to influence from neighbours and donors. Watch for foreign-funded advisers placed in ministries, as happened in Indonesia.

Turkiye.d: Türkiye has the highest documented score on this map, with records running from the Cold War to the 2016 coup attempt. Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit said he learned of the Counter-Guerrilla, NATO's stay-behind unit in the army's Special Warfare Department, when General Kemal Yamak asked him for money after US funding ended around 1973–74; Grey Wolves leader Alparslan Turkes was deputy prime minister in 1975–78. On 3 November 1996 a Mercedes that crashed near Susurluk was found to be carrying a deputy Istanbul police chief, an MP and Grey Wolves fugitive Abdullah Catli; Catli carried a false passport and gun licence signed by Interior Minister Mehmet Agar, who resigned, and parliament's inquiry concluded in April 1997 that state bodies had used the Grey Wolves. The Sledgehammer and Ergenekon trials of 2012–13 convicted about 300 officers, a former army chief and three opposition MPs of coup plots, but the courts reversed both: all 236 remaining Sledgehammer defendants were acquitted in March 2015 after the evidence was found forged, and the Court of Cassation found in April 2016 no evidence that Ergenekon existed; the government now blames those prosecutions on Gülen-linked police and prosecutors. After a December 2013 graft probe reached Erdogan's inner circle, the government called it a Gülen plot, dismissed the four lead prosecutors and moved around 1,000 police; after the 15 July 2016 coup attempt it removed 2,745 judges in one day, about 15,000 military personnel, about 23,000 police and about 150,000 public employees by decree, and courts gave former air force commander Akin Ozturk multiple aggravated life terms and 337 Akinci base defendants life sentences. Abroad, a Turkish official said in June 2021 that Interpol had refused 773 Turkish Red Notice requests on Gülen suspects as political. Türkiye is headquarters of the Gülen movement, the Grey Wolves and the alleged Ergenekon network; it appears in 'The anticommunist web', 'Faith movements placing members in the state' (as the purging state), 'Exposure, purge and reversal' (including court reversals) and 'Governments and industries inside international bodies', and its pursuit of Gülen-linked schools and staff abroad links it to the cases in Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Malaysia, Pakistan and Tajikistan.
Turkiye.imp: For decades people in the army, police and a nationalist street movement worked together out of public view, and a parliamentary inquiry confirmed that state bodies used that movement. Later, courts convicted hundreds of officers and then found the evidence forged; the government now says a religious movement inside the police and courts ran those cases, and after 2016 it dismissed about 150,000 public employees on that basis, mostly by decree rather than individual trial. Citizens have had to weigh competing claims of infiltration from each side. Watch for mass dismissals without hearings and for evidence that cannot be tested in court.

Turkmenistan.d: Turkmenistan closed or nationalised most of the Gülen-linked schools opened in the 1990s in 2011. After more than 100 people, most with some Gülen affiliation, were detained in late 2016, 18 men were convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and involvement in a criminal organisation, according to a joint statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee. The map lists Turkmenistan in 'Faith movements placing members in the state'. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta also has documented presence.
Turkmenistan.imp: The record shows a closed state jailing people over a religious affiliation in trials the public could not attend, and what the courts found is known only through rights groups. Watch for convictions without open evidence.

United Arab Emirates.d: By 5 July 1991 the Abu Dhabi government, its ruling family and their investment company owned 77% of BCCI. Ghanim Al Mazrui, secretary general of the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, sat on BCCI's board from 1981 and later chaired it; the US Senate Kerry–Brown report of 1992 found Abu Dhabi was told of the bank's fraud in April 1990, kept it from the auditors until November 1990, and gave evasive and misleading answers. That makes the UAE the bank headquarters in 'Banks that carried the hidden money'. At home, the Federal Supreme Court on 2 July 2013 jailed 56 of the 'UAE 94', many from the Islah group, for a plot to overthrow the government that the Attorney General said included infiltrating ministries, schools and universities, sentenced 8 in absentia and acquitted 26; Islah denies organisational ties to the Brotherhood, and in November 2014 the cabinet listed both as terrorist, placing the UAE in 'Movements that sought the state itself'. Abroad, the UAE gave donations reported at about $54 million through the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World, estimated to equal the statutory contributions of the other 194 members combined, and Interior Ministry inspector general Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi was elected Interpol president on 25 November 2021; in March 2022 French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry into torture complaints against him, which the UAE denies. These place the UAE in 'Governments and industries inside international bodies' and 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
United Arab Emirates.imp: The UAE appears here as an owner and user of hidden channels: its rulers owned most of a bank that hid fraud, and its money and officials reached the top of Interpol. The torture complaints against Al-Raisi are at the inquiry stage, not a finding. Watch for large donations to international bodies by governments that then seek to lead them.

Uzbekistan.d: No case is documented on this map for Uzbekistan, and no tracked organisation has documented presence; the Gülen movement, Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Grey Wolves are listed as likely present. State-embedded actors score 7 of 10 and resilience 3.8. As an estimate, the most likely activity follows the region's two recorded patterns: Turkey's pursuit of Gülen-linked schools, documented in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan, and Hizb ut-Tahrir recruitment.
Uzbekistan.imp: With weak checks, either a foreign government's requests or a banned movement's recruits could reach officials without a public record. Watch the security services and schools.

Vietnam.d: This map records no case for Vietnam. Opus Dei is the only tracked organisation with documented presence. State-embedded actors score 7 of 10 and resilience 4.8. As a best-judgement estimate, outside reach would most likely come through Chinese state networks; the Australian conviction of Di Sanh Duong involved a federation of Chinese organisations for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.
Vietnam.imp: No office has been shown to be reached. Watch overseas community federations that link diaspora groups to foreign agencies.

Yemen.d: No case is documented on this map for Yemen. The Muslim Brotherhood has documented presence and Hizb ut-Tahrir is likely present. State-embedded actors score 8 of 10 and resilience 1.9, among the lowest in this file. As an estimate, outside reach would most likely come through movements tied to regional powers; Saudi Arabia's 2014 terrorist list named the Houthis alongside the Brotherhood.
Yemen.imp: With almost no working checks, armed and foreign-backed groups can hold power without leaving a record. The empty record here is a gap in evidence, not a sign of absence.

Australia.d: Australia's record centres on Huang Xiangmo, a property developer who chaired the Australian Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China from 2014 to 2017, a body described as a peak group for United Front-linked organisations. Labor senator Sam Dastyari had a Huang-linked company pay his legal bills, told a June 2016 press conference with Huang present that China's borders were 'a matter for China', reportedly warned Huang his phone was probably tapped, and resigned in January 2018. In February 2019 the government cancelled Huang's permanent residency on ASIO advice that he was 'amenable to conducting acts of foreign interference'; with associates he had given about AU$2 million to Labor and over AU$1 million to the Liberal Party. On 28 February 2022 the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption found that $100,000 in cash delivered to NSW Labor in 2015 came from Huang, disguised as staff donations, and that former MP Ernest Wong engaged in corrupt conduct. On 19 December 2023 Melbourne community leader Di Sanh Duong became the first person convicted under the 2018 foreign interference law, for using community roles to reach acting immigration minister Alan Tudge while concealing links to the United Front, the Ministry of State Security and the Chinese consulate. These make Australia a target country in 'One state's networks inside another'. It is also headquarters of Nugan Hand Bank, which collapsed in 1980 with retired senior US military and intelligence officers on its staff ('Banks that carried the hidden money'), a Round Table dominion group from 1910, and the case of Tim Wilson, who went from the Atlas-partner Institute of Public Affairs to Human Rights Commissioner in 2014 and later assistant minister ('Private forums where officials meet money').
Australia.imp: One donor's money reached both main parties, a senator and a state party office before security agencies acted, and the public learned of it through a resignation, an anti-corruption report and a court case. Australia then passed a law that produced its first conviction in 2023. Watch large donors who hold roles in reunification councils or community federations, and how their donations are routed.

Fiji.d: No case is documented on this map for Fiji. Shincheonji has documented presence, and India's RSS is likely present. State-embedded actors score 4 of 10 and resilience 5.4. As an estimate, the most likely outside reach is through religious movements that move members into party politics, as Korean prosecutors allege Shincheonji did with South Korea's governing party, and through RSS-linked diaspora groups.
Fiji.imp: Nothing has been shown inside government. Watch for mass sign-ups to political parties by religious groups.

Kiribati.d: This map records no case for Kiribati. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the only tracked organisation with documented presence. State-embedded actors score very low (1.5 of 10) and resilience sits just below the middle (4.5). As an estimate, outside influence would most likely come from larger states competing for ties, through aid, donations and paid trips of the kind documented in the Taiwan and Australia cases.
Kiribati.imp: No case means no documented reach, not proof of none. Watch foreign-funded trips and donations to officials.

Marshall Islands.d: No case is documented on this map for the Marshall Islands. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has documented presence, and no other tracked organisation is listed. State-embedded actors score low (2.5 of 10) and resilience fairly well (5.7). As a best-judgement estimate, outside influence would come through competition between larger states, such as the China–Taiwan rivalry visible in Taiwan's cases.
Marshall Islands.imp: Nothing is documented. Watch paid trips for local leaders, a method Taiwanese courts have punished.

Micronesia.d: This map holds no case for Micronesia. Its only tracked organisation with documented presence is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta. State-embedded actors score low (3 of 10) and resilience moderate (5.5). As an estimate, the most likely outside reach would come through aid, donations and sponsored travel from larger states.
Micronesia.imp: No reach has been shown. In a small government a few large gifts can matter, so watch who pays for officials' travel and campaigns.

Nauru.d: No case is documented on this map for Nauru. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has documented presence. State-embedded actors score 3.5 of 10 and resilience 4.8. As an estimate, outside influence would most likely come through payments from larger states and their contractors.
Nauru.imp: Nothing is documented. Watch foreign payments that are tied to government decisions.

New Zealand.d: New Zealand's three cases concern forums and think tanks, and none involves a finding of wrongdoing. Ruth Richardson, Finance Minister from November 1990 to 1993, is listed as a Mont Pelerin Society member and sat on its board in 2018–20. Jacinda Ardern, Prime Minister from 2017 to 2023, is listed by the German Bundestag's research service among participants in the WEF's Forum of Young Global Leaders, a WEF selection rather than a finding of influence. David Seymour worked in the 2000s for Canadian think tanks including the Frontier Centre for Public Policy, an Atlas Network partner, and became ACT leader in 2014, Minister for Regulation in 2023 and Deputy Prime Minister in 2025; Atlas chair Debbi Gibbs is the daughter of ACT co-founder Alan Gibbs. No forum has found that any of these networks directed government decisions. All three place New Zealand in 'Private forums where officials meet money', and it has been a Round Table dominion group since 1910.
New Zealand.imp: A finance minister, a prime minister and a deputy prime minister each passed through international policy networks that most voters do not follow. That is lawful, and no influence has been found. Watch the family link between Atlas's chair and the ACT party, and whether regulation policy tracks think-tank proposals.

Palau.d: This map documents no case and no tracked organisation for Palau. State-embedded actors score 3.5 of 10 and resilience 5.1. As an estimate, outside influence would most likely come through rival larger states seeking diplomatic support, using the paid trips and donations seen in the Taiwan and Australia cases.
Palau.imp: The record is empty. Sponsored travel and donations to local leaders are the methods to watch.

Papua New Guinea.d: No case is documented on this map for Papua New Guinea, and no tracked organisation has documented or likely presence. State-embedded actors score 8.5 of 10 and resilience 3.2, the weakest conditions in the Pacific part of this file. As an estimate, outside reach would most likely come through foreign companies and states working with officials who already hold private interests.
Papua New Guinea.imp: When insiders already profit from office, outsiders can buy access without appearing in any membership list. The empty record reflects that gap.

Samoa.d: This map records no case for Samoa. Shincheonji has documented presence. State-embedded actors score low (2.5 of 10) and resilience is among the stronger in the Pacific (5.9). As an estimate, any reach would most likely come through religious movements moving members into politics, as prosecutors allege Shincheonji did in South Korea.
Samoa.imp: Nothing is shown. Watch whether church groups sign members up to parties or organise their votes.

Solomon Islands.d: No case is documented on this map for Solomon Islands, and no tracked organisation is listed. State-embedded actors score fairly high (7.5 of 10) and resilience 4.7. As an estimate, outside influence would most likely come through larger states' aid and payments to politicians, of the kind documented in Australia's United Front cases.
Solomon Islands.imp: With strong insider interests, influence could pass through payments rather than organisations. Watch money from foreign sources to members of parliament.

Tonga.d: This map records no case for Tonga and no tracked organisation. State-embedded actors score 6 of 10 and resilience 5.2. As a best-judgement estimate, the most likely outside reach would come through loans, aid and donations from larger states.
Tonga.imp: The empty record does not rule out influence. Watch foreign loans and the officials who arrange them.

Tuvalu.d: No case is documented on this map for Tuvalu, and no tracked organisation is present. Its conditions are among the better ones in this file: state-embedded actors 1.5 of 10 and resilience 5.9. As an estimate, outside influence would most likely come through diplomatic competition between larger states rather than hidden networks.
Tuvalu.imp: Nothing has been documented. Watch sponsored travel and donations for officials.

Vanuatu.d: This map records no case for Vanuatu and no tracked organisation. State-embedded actors score low (3 of 10) and resilience 4.9. As a best-judgement estimate, outside reach would most likely come through aid and payments from larger states or foreign firms.
Vanuatu.imp: No reach has been shown. Watch payments and gifts to officials from foreign states or companies.

Albania.d: No case of a secret society or international organisation reaching inside Albania's government is documented on this map. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has a documented presence, and the Gülen movement is listed as likely present but undocumented. The conditions scores show a fairly high level of state-embedded actors (6.5 of 10) and middling resilience (5.2 of 10). As a best-judgement estimate, any outside reach would most likely run through networks already embedded in state bodies, or through foreign-linked movements such as Gülen's schools and associations, rather than through a lodge.
Albania.imp: Nothing on this map shows a hidden network steering Albania's government. The scores point to officials tied to outside interests as the weaker spot, so the things to watch are how public posts are filled and whether foreign-backed movements gain places in schools or ministries.

Andorra.d: Andorra has no documented case on this map. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the only organisation with a documented presence, and none of the map's cross-border patterns touches the country. Its conditions scores are among the strongest in Europe: very few state-embedded actors (1.0 of 10) and high resilience (8.0 of 10). As an estimate, any reach would most likely come through foreign money using its financial sector rather than through a society placing members in office.
Andorra.imp: The record gives no sign of hidden control in Andorra. If influence were sought, the likeliest route is outside money looking for friendly officials, which is where scrutiny would matter most.

Austria.d: In 1951 trade unionist Franz Olah set up a secret anti-communist paramilitary force under the cover name OeWSGV, funded through the camouflage firms Atlanta and Omnia; it ran until 1964. Olah became president of the ÖGB union federation in 1959 and Interior Minister in 1963, resigned in September 1964 over misuse of union funds, and at his 1969 fraud trial, which ended in a one-year sentence, defended the force as a patriotic measure. As late as 1991 Austria's defence and interior ministers denied that such an army had existed. In January 1996 reports revealed more than 80 hidden US arms caches left in Austria for an early Cold War stay-behind network; Austrian officials said they had not been told, and when the government's historian Oliver Rathkolb sought more US documents, the CIA said none were available. Austria is a documented case in the anticommunist web of 1945–1990. In the pattern of private forums where officials meet money, the Bundestag research service lists Chancellor Sebastian Kurz as a WEF Young Global Leaders participant, a WEF selection that no forum has found directed his decisions.
Austria.imp: For more than a decade a secret armed force raised by a man who became Interior Minister existed in Austria, and a foreign power kept over 80 weapons stores on Austrian soil without telling the government. Ministers still denied the force in 1991. The thing to watch is whether remaining records on these networks are released, and whether official denials hold up against documents.

Belarus.d: No case is documented for Belarus on this map. Belarus scores very high on state-embedded actors (9.0 of 10) and low on resilience (3.1 of 10). As a best-judgement estimate, outside reach would most likely come from Russian state bodies such as Russkiy Mir, which this map places in the pattern of one state's networks inside another, rather than from private societies.
Belarus.imp: The absence of a documented case reflects a closed state where independent inquiries are rare, not proof that no influence exists. With power concentrated and weak checks, influence would be hard for citizens to see, and it would most likely come from a neighbouring state's agencies.

Belgium.d: Westland New Post, a far-right group active from 1981, was founded by Paul Latinus, a former informant for State Security; State Security agent Christian Smets admitted training its members in surveillance, and the service had a mole in the group from 1981 without telling the police. Former gendarme Martin Leukeu said he was recruited into 'Group G', a neo-Nazi cell inside the Gendarmerie linked to the group, and NATO documents from the Evere transmission centre were found at a member's home; a parliamentary inquiry found no proof of a conspiracy behind the Brabant killings. Belgium's stay-behind network was made public on 7 November 1990 and the government decided to disband it on 23 November. A Senate commission chaired by Roger Lallemand heard 37 witnesses in 1991, described a military section (SDRA VIII), a civilian section (STC/Mob) and a coordination secretariat funded by secret NATO payments, and criticised the refusal to name civilian operatives. Belgium is a documented case in the anticommunist web, an example of a parliament exposing such a network, and the listed headquarters of the stay-behind coordination bodies. In the private-forums pattern, Alexander De Croo was named a WEF Young Global Leader in 2015 while Deputy Prime Minister and became Prime Minister in 2020, a WEF selection rather than a finding of influence.
Belgium.imp: Belgian security services had an informant, a trainer and a mole connected to an armed far-right group and did not share what they knew with the police. A secret network paid for partly by NATO ran outside public view until 1990, and even the Senate inquiry could not get the names of its civilian members. The thing to watch is whether intelligence services report to police and parliament what they know about armed groups.

Czech Republic.d: Václav Klaus, a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, was Czechoslovak Finance Minister from December 1989, Czech Prime Minister from 1993 to 1997 and President from 2003 to 2013; membership and office are documented, but no forum has found that the society directed his decisions. On 27 March 2024 Petr Fiala's government put the Voice of Europe network, Viktor Medvedchuk and Artyom Marchevsky on the national sanctions list after the BIS security service said the network was financed from Russia and operated on Czech territory. Deník N, citing a foreign ministry source, reported that payments went to politicians from Belgium, France, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Poland, in particular the AfD. The BIS account of a recorded Prague meeting led Munich prosecutors to investigate AfD Bundestag member Petr Bystron, who denies receiving money. The Czech Republic is the target country in the pattern of one state's networks inside another and the government that banned the network in the exposure-and-purge pattern; it appears in the private-forums pattern through Klaus.
Czech Republic.imp: The Czech case concerns a foreign state using a news outlet based in Prague to pass money to politicians across Europe, uncovered by Czech intelligence and acted on by sanctions rather than a court verdict. Readers of the outlet could not see who paid for it. Watch the court outcomes in the countries whose politicians were named, and who funds similar outlets.

Denmark.d: Denmark's stay-behind network, code-named Absalon and led by E. J. Harder, was hidden inside the military intelligence service Forsvarets Efterretningstjeneste, according to historians cited by Wikipedia. Time reported in November 1990 that the Danish and Norwegian units had been built 'with official cooperation', and The Guardian reported in January 1992 that Denmark was among the countries that investigated and disbanded their networks after Italy's disclosure. Denmark is a documented case in the anticommunist web of 1945–1990. Other bodies documented as present, including the World Anti-Communist League, Bilderberg, the Trilateral Commission and the Mont Pelerin Society, have no case on this map.
Denmark.imp: A secret network sat inside Denmark's military intelligence service for decades, and the public learned of it only after Italy's 1990 disclosure. The sources here are press reports and historians rather than a published Danish report, so the full picture is still not public. Watch whether the Absalon files are opened.
