Finland.d: After the Moscow Armistice of 19 September 1944, Colonel Valo Nihtilä and Lieutenant Colonel Usko Haahti of the operational department of Finnish Military Headquarters began hiding weapons across the country, planned for 8,000 men but estimated to equip about 35,000, with 5,000 to 10,000 people taking part. The scheme was exposed to the Allied Control Commission in spring 1945; the security police questioned more than 5,000 people and, under a retroactive law of January 1947, 1,488 people were convicted, most receiving one to four months in prison. Finland is a documented case in the anticommunist web of 1945–1990 and the home of the weapons cache network. In the private-forums pattern, the Bundestag research service lists Prime Minister Sanna Marin (2019–23) as a WEF Young Global Leaders participant, a WEF selection that no forum has found directed her decisions.
Finland.imp: Officers at military headquarters armed a hidden force of up to 35,000 people without public knowledge, and it took a foreign control commission and a law written after the fact to prosecute it. The case shows how far an armed service could act on its own in a period of crisis. Watch how military stockpiles and reserve networks are overseen by parliament.

France.d: Between 1901 and 1904 War Minister General Louis André used reports gathered through Grand Orient de France lodges to sort army officers for promotion, with 18,818 files counted by historian Serge Berstein; André resigned on 15 November 1904 after the scheme was exposed in the Chamber, and the Combes government fell in January 1905. In 1960 Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, co-founded the Service d'Action Civique; after an SAC commando murdered Marseille police inspector and local SAC leader Jacques Massié and his family at Auriol in 1981, a National Assembly inquiry reported and the government dissolved the SAC by decree in August 1982. Generals led by Raoul Salan formed the clandestine OAS after the failed 1961 Algiers putsch; Salan was sentenced to life for treason in 1962, pardoned in 1968 and reinstated as a general in 1982. Former Prime Minister Antoine Pinay founded Le Cercle in 1952–53 with Jean Violet, with Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss counted as co-founders by historian Adrian Hänni, and the CIA ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom from Paris through officer Michael Josselson, which former CIA official Thomas Braden admitted in 1967. According to L'Express, Manuel Valls was a Grand Orient lodge member from 1989 to 2005, the years in which he became mayor of Évry and a deputy, before serving as Interior Minister and Prime Minister; he declined to answer the magazine. France is the lodge centre in the pattern linking French lodges to African presidencies, in which the GLNF's grand master installed Ali Bongo as grand master of Gabon's lodge in 2009 and Foccart's SAC ran Africa networks from the Élysée; it is also a documented case in the anticommunist web and the place the money went in the CIA-funded NGO pattern. In the private-forums pattern, WEF lists Nicolas Sarkozy among its 1993 Global Leaders for Tomorrow and the Bundestag research service lists Emmanuel Macron as a Young Global Leaders alumnus, selections no forum has found directed their decisions.
France.imp: The French record includes a lodge sorting army officers for a minister, a militia founded by the president's Africa adviser that was dissolved only after it murdered one of its own leaders, and a cultural body whose CIA funding was hidden for over ten years. Each came out through a parliamentary exposure, an inquiry or the press, years after the fact. Lodge membership on its own, as in the Valls report, is lawful and no forum found misconduct. The ties between French lodges and the leaders of former colonies are the thread to keep watching.

Germany.d: Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke states that Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank were members of Munich's Thule Society before rising in the Nazi Party; Hess became Deputy Führer in 1933 and Frank a Reich minister and, from 1939, Governor-General of occupied Poland. In 1981 forester Heinz Lembke led investigators to 33 illegal arms dumps on the Lüneburg Heath holding 156 kg of explosives and 50 anti-tank weapons; he was found hanged in his cell the day before a hearing at which he had said he would name his backers, and a link to NATO stay-behind stocks was suggested but never confirmed. On 17 May 1991 the federal government told the Bundestag that the BND's stay-behind organisation was being dissolved, while disputing the European Parliament's 1990 resolution as resting on incorrect premises for Germany; from Munich, Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty had broadcast on CIA money until 1971–72. In July 2020 domestic intelligence put Uniter, an association founded by former KSK soldier André Schmitt, under surveillance, the same week a KSK company was disbanded after explosives and an AK-47 were found on a sergeant major's property. In December 2022 Berlin judge and former AfD MP Birgit Malsack-Winkemann was arrested in the raids on the Reuss group, which prosecutors say planned to storm the Reichstag with up to 16 people mainly from special units and to make her justice minister; 26 defendants have been on trial since 2024, with no verdict reported as of April 2026. In 2024 Munich prosecutors opened a bribery inquiry into AfD member Petr Bystron over Voice of Europe cash described in a Czech intelligence briefing; he denies it and no charge had been reported. Germany is a documented case in the anticommunist web, a brotherhood example through Thule, the target country of Russia's network, the place the money went for the CIA-funded radios, and appears in the private-forums pattern through Ludwig Erhard, a Mont Pelerin member while Economics Minister from 1950, and Angela Merkel, a 1993 WEF Global Leader for Tomorrow, neither found to have been directed by those bodies.
Germany.imp: Germany's cases run from a pre-war society whose members reached the top of the Nazi state to recent networks of soldiers, police and a sitting judge accused of preparing a takeover. Key questions remain open: Lembke's backers were never named, and the Reuss trials and the Bystron inquiry had not ended in verdicts or charges. Watch the outcomes of those cases and how special forces and judges are screened for such ties.

Greece.d: IDEA, a secret society of army officers formed in 1945 by veterans of the collaborationist Security Battalions, called dictatorship the only solution for Greece in its 1952 manifesto; several leaders of the 21 April 1967 coup, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and members took key posts under the junta. During the coup the LOK mountain raiding companies, part of the European stay-behind network since 1952, seized the Defence Ministry under Brigadier General Kostas Aslanides. In 1975 a court sentenced Papadopoulos, Stylianos Pattakos and Nikolaos Makarezos to death for high treason, commuted to life, and gave former military police head Dimitrios Ioannidis life. In 1990 the defence minister confirmed that a stay-behind branch, Operation Sheepskin, had operated until 1988; Andreas Papandreou said he had learned of it in 1984 and ordered it dissolved. After the May 2012 election, polling stations used by Attica police officers showed just over 20% for Golden Dawn against about 6% at civilian stations, and in 2013 the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner said he had strong evidence of ties between police and the party. In 2020 the Athens Court of Appeals found Golden Dawn's leader and six other leading members guilty of directing a criminal organisation, upheld for 42 defendants in March 2026. Greece is the clearest European case of a sworn brotherhood running the government, and a documented case in the anticommunist web in which the officers' society and the stay-behind unit acted together in the coup.
Greece.imp: From 1967 to 1974 Greece was ruled by officers from a secret society, with a special forces unit tied to the NATO stay-behind network seizing the Defence Ministry for them, and courts later convicted the leaders of treason. Decades later, police voting returns and the Council of Europe pointed to ties between police and a party a court found to be a criminal organisation. Watch how the army and police check recruits' political ties.

Hungarian politicians were among those Deník N reported received Voice of Europe payments (see the Czech Republic entry), though no Hungarian case is recorded here. With a fairly high level of state-embedded actors (7.5 of 10) and resilience below the middle (4.8), the most likely sources of outside reach, as a best-judgement estimate, are foreign-state funding of politicians and networks already embedded in the governing apparatus.
Hungary.imp: The map does not document hidden control in Hungary, but the weak resilience score means it would be hard for citizens to see. The Voice of Europe reports show the route to watch: outside money reaching politicians through media fronts.

Iceland.imp: Nothing on the map shows a hidden network inside Iceland's government. If records exist, they would most likely concern Cold War defence arrangements that were never made public.

Ireland.d: John A. Costello, Taoiseach of the first Inter-Party government from 1948, was a member of the Knights of Saint Columbanus, a Catholic order headquartered in Ireland; with other cabinet members who were also Knights, his government gave Maynooth seminary a special annual grant. Labour parliamentary chairman William Davin TD, also a Knight, is reported to have countered support within government for the Mother and Child health scheme, which Archbishop John Charles McQuaid opposed. Justice Minister Seán MacEoin, another member, reportedly assured the Order's Supreme Council that efforts would be made to prevent conflict between Church and State. The Order also had members in the civil service, including Dublin City chief planner Michael O'Brien and the Taxing Master of the Courts, Henry B. O'Hanlon. These accounts rest chiefly on John Cooney's 1999 biography of McQuaid and Anthony Jordan's 2007 biography of Costello, not on an inquiry. Ireland is a case in the pattern of sworn brotherhoods holding key offices.
Ireland.imp: In 1948 the head of government, the justice minister and other ministers belonged to a Catholic fraternal order, and the justice minister reportedly gave the order assurances about Church and State. Citizens would not have known these ties when a public health scheme opposed by the archbishop was debated. The account comes from biographers rather than a court or inquiry. Watch whether office holders disclose membership of bodies that take positions on the laws they handle.

Italy.d: On 17 March 1981 financial police sent by Milan magistrates investigating banker Michele Sindona searched Licio Gelli's factory at Castiglion Fibocchi and found the membership list of the P2 lodge: 962 names, including 44 members of parliament, ministers, 195 military officers, Chief of Defence Staff Admiral Giovanni Torrisi, Guardia di Finanza commander Orazio Giannini and the heads of all three intelligence bodies (Giuseppe Santovito of SISMI, Giulio Grassini of SISDE and Walter Pelosi of CESIS). Prime Minister Arnaldo Forlani's government fell in May 1981 after he was accused of delaying the list's publication; sitting ministers Enrico Manca and Franco Foschi were on it, and the SISMI and SISDE directors were removed or resigned. The Anselmi parliamentary commission (1981–84) called P2 a criminal and subversive organisation, and Law 17 of 1982 dissolved it and banned secret associations that seek to interfere with public bodies, although a Rome court acquitted Gelli and others of conspiracy against the state in 1994, confirmed in 1996. P2 members ran the banks at the centre of the money trail: Sindona, who advised the Vatican on its investments, was sentenced to life in 1986 as instigator of the 1979 murder of Giorgio Ambrosoli, the lawyer liquidating his banks, and Banco Ambrosiano, chaired by P2 member Roberto Calvi, collapsed in 1982 with about US$1.287 billion missing, much of it routed through offshore companies tied to its main shareholder, the Vatican Bank (IOR). Calvi was found hanged under Blackfriars Bridge in London in June 1982; a Rome court in 2007 treated the death as murder while acquitting five defendants, and Gelli's 12-year sentence for the Ambrosiano fraud was confirmed in 1998. Courts also tied P2 figures to the Bologna station bombing of 1980, which killed 85 people: Gelli and SISMI officers including General Pietro Musumeci were convicted in 1995 for planting false evidence to divert the inquiry, and in the Bellini case, made final in 2025, appeal judges called Gelli the 'knowing financier' of the massacre; Silvio Berlusconi, later prime minister three times, was on the 1981 list, and in 1990 a Venice appeal court found his account of brief membership was false testimony but could not sentence him because of an amnesty. On 24 October 1990 Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti told parliament that the NATO-coordinated stay-behind network Gladio had existed since the 1950s, with 622 civilians on its list; the disclosure followed Venice magistrate Felice Casson's reopening of the 1972 Peteano car bombing, and President Francesco Cossiga acknowledged a role in setting it up. Later cases followed the lodges and the 1982 law: in 2018 a Rome court convicted Flavio Carboni of secret association in the 'P3' case, in which former First President of the Court of Cassation Vincenzo Carbone received a suspended sentence for abuse of office, and in 2011 the 'P4' inquiry led to the arrest of deputy and former prosecutor Alfonso Papa, whose conviction lapsed on appeal before he was removed from the bench in 2023. In December 2017 the Anti-Mafia Commission reported 193 lodge members recorded in organised-crime proceedings, found that 4 of the 5 town assessors in Castelvetrano, Matteo Messina Denaro's home town, were Masons in 2016, and recommended barring magistrates, career soldiers and police from lodges, though the European Court of Human Rights held its seizure of lodge lists breached privacy; in 2023 former senator Giancarlo Pittelli, described by prosecutors as a Mason linking an 'Ndrangheta clan to Masonic circles, received 11 years for collusion. Italy is the coordinating centre of the anticommunist web, where stay-behind and lodge networks overlapped most, the headquarters of the banks that carried the hidden money, and the largest documented case of lodges inside police, intelligence and courts; in the private-forums pattern it lists Mont Pelerin members Luigi Einaudi (President, 1948–55) and Antonio Martino (Foreign and Defence Minister), and in the faith-movements pattern Communion and Liberation figure Roberto Formigoni, whose 2019 corruption conviction concerned bribes, not the movement.
Italy.imp: In 1981 one private lodge counted among its members the heads of every intelligence service, the chief of defence staff, the commander of the financial police, ministers and dozens of MPs, and the public learned this only because magistrates investigating a banker found the list. Courts later tied P2 figures to a bank collapse, a murder and the diversion of a massacre inquiry, though the charge that the lodge conspired against the state ended in acquittal. Citizens could not see that officials responsible for investigating these crimes belonged to the same lodge as some of the suspects. The things to watch now are disclosure of lodge membership by magistrates, police and the military, and how the 1982 secret-associations law is applied to lodges tied to organised crime.

Luxembourg.d: In 2013 two former members of the Gendarmerie's mobile brigade, Jos Wilmes and Marc Scheer, went on trial for 18 bombings in Luxembourg between May 1984 and April 1986, including attacks on power pylons. The defence argued the attacks were the work of NATO's stay-behind network, and a 2006 recording of Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, Justice Minister Luc Frieden and intelligence chief Marco Mille speculating about stay-behind involvement was played in court. Prosecutor Robert Biever said 88 of 125 pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended in 2014; eight former gendarmerie and public-force officers were later referred to trial for false testimony, but not for the bombings. Luxembourg is a documented case in the anticommunist web, and in the pattern of banks that carried hidden money it is where BCCI Holdings was registered before regulators closed the bank on 5 July 1991.
Luxembourg.imp: A bombing campaign was charged against police officers, the country's own prime minister and intelligence chief were recorded speculating about a secret NATO network's role, and most of the evidence went missing. No court has found who carried out the bombings. Watch whether the false-testimony proceedings and any surviving records answer that.

Netherlands.d: In November 1990 Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers told parliament that the Dutch stay-behind network was being given a new direction, and in April 1992 Defence Minister Relus ter Beek wrote that it had become obsolete. The network, run through secret Intelligence (I) and Operations (O) units, operated from 1945 to 1992 with several hundred recruited citizens and dozens of weapons caches; according to de Volkskrant, the government covered up the theft of some guns later used by members of Willem Holleeder's gang. In February 2021 Prime Minister Mark Rutte and Defence Minister Ank Bijleveld acknowledged the group in a letter to relatives, and in 2022 the government asked the Netherlands Institute for Military History to inventory its records. The Netherlands is a documented case in the anticommunist web of 1945–1990 and, as home of the Bilderberg Meetings, the headquarters entry in the pattern of private forums where officials meet money; no Bilderberg case is recorded here.
Netherlands.imp: Several hundred citizens were recruited into a secret network with weapons caches for almost 50 years, and the government only wrote to their relatives about it in 2021. If de Volkskrant is right, weapons from the network reached a criminal gang and the theft was covered up. Watch what the military history institute's inventory makes public.

Norway.d: In 1978 Norwegian police found an arms cache and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested businessman Hans Otto Meyer, who said Norwegian intelligence had supplied the weapons. Defence Minister Rolf Hansen then said the stay-behind network 'was not in any way answerable to NATO and had no CIA connection'. In 1957 intelligence chief Vilhelm Evang had protested to NATO about stay-behind activity by officers at the Kolsås headquarters, a dispute settled in 1958 with assurances on how the networks would be run. Norway is a documented case in the anticommunist web of 1945–1990; Time reported in 1990 that the Danish and Norwegian units were built 'with official cooperation'.
Norway.imp: Norway's network came to light by accident, when police found weapons supplied by the intelligence service in a private citizen's hands. Its own intelligence chief had earlier complained that NATO officers were acting on stay-behind matters in Norway. Watch whether the full records of who controlled the network are released.

Poland.d: Aleksander Stępkowski co-founded the Catholic legal institute Ordo Iuris in 2013 and chaired its board in 2013–2015; in November 2015 Beata Szydło's new Law and Justice government made him deputy foreign minister for legal and treaty affairs, and he was recalled in August 2016. In 2016 Ordo Iuris drafted a near-total abortion ban that the Sejm rejected on 6 October 2016 after nationwide protests. Stępkowski, back as board president in 2016–2017, was nominated to the Supreme Court in 2018 by the reconstituted National Council of the Judiciary and appointed in February 2019 with no prior judicial experience. On 15 May 2020 President Andrzej Duda entrusted him with the duties of acting First President of the Supreme Court. Poland, where Ordo Iuris is headquartered, is a case in the pattern of faith movements placing members in the state.
Poland.imp: The co-founder of an advocacy group that drafted one of Poland's most contested bills moved into the foreign ministry and then, without judicial experience, to the temporary head of the Supreme Court. These were lawful appointments, and the dossier records no finding of misconduct. Watch how advocacy-group leaders are appointed to courts and whether their ties are weighed in cases their group cares about.

Portugal.d: Aginter Press was set up in Lisbon in September 1966 under Salazar's Estado Novo and run by former French officer and OAS member Yves Guérin-Sérac; it presented itself as a press agency but trained members in bombing and sabotage. Its documents were found at the end of 1974 after the Carnation Revolution, when Guérin-Sérac and associates left Portugal. In 1997 Italian magistrate Guido Salvini told Italy's parliamentary terrorism commission that his Piazza Fontana inquiry confirmed links between Aginter, Ordine Nuovo and Avanguardia Nazionale, and that Aginter instructors taught Avanguardia Nazionale members to use explosives in Rome in 1967–68. Portugal is a documented case in the anticommunist web and an example of exposure by a parliamentary commission, with the OAS link tying it to France and the Salvini findings tying it to Italy's bombings. In the private-forums pattern, WEF lists José Manuel Durão Barroso, Prime Minister in 2002–04 and later European Commission president, among its 1993 Global Leaders for Tomorrow, a selection that no forum has found directed his decisions.
Portugal.imp: Under the dictatorship, a group calling itself a news agency trained people in bombing, and an Italian magistrate later traced its teaching to the groups behind Italy's bombings. Its records surfaced only when the regime fell. Watch for organisations that use media or research labels as cover for security work.

Romania.d: In September 2019 Newsweek România reported, citing anonymous Masonic sources, that Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, joined Freemasonry in 2008 through Loja Armonia and later Loja Basarab, and that General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie, belonged to Loja Basarab. Neither had declared membership in his interest declarations, which the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied; Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was. The claim rests on that one outlet. Romania appears on the map through this case only and is not part of a listed cross-border pattern.
Romania.imp: If the report is accurate, the minister in charge of the police and the head of the Gendarmerie belonged to the same lodge and did not declare it as the magazine said the law required. No court or inquiry has tested the claim. Watch whether interest declarations are enforced for security officials.

Russia.d: Alexander Kerensky was Secretary General of the Masonic Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples from 1916 to mid-1917, after Nikolai Nekrasov, and in 1917 served in the Provisional Government as Minister of Justice, Minister for War and then Prime Minister; historians describe most of the lodge's members as associated with that government. In July 2015 Russia declared the US National Endowment for Democracy the first 'undesirable' organisation under a new law, with officials blaming NED grants for the 2014 Euromaidan protests in Ukraine; no court or independent body has found that NED worked inside Russian state institutions. Interpol refused Russia's repeated requests for a Red Notice against financier Bill Browder as 'predominantly political', and in November 2018 four US senators said Interpol vice-president Alexander Prokopchuk, a Russian Interior Ministry general, had abused Red Notices before he lost the presidency vote. In January 2026 the BBC reported leaked files showing Interpol received more complaints about Russia than any other country. Russia is the sponsoring state in the pattern of one state's networks inside another, through the Russkiy Mir Foundation (2007) and the Voice of Europe network sanctioned by the Czech government in 2024 for paying European politicians, and the government involved in the pattern of governments inside international bodies through its use of Interpol.
Russia.imp: Russia appears on this map mainly as a state reaching into others: funding a network that paid European politicians and using a police body's notices against critics abroad. The NED ban is the Russian government's own claim, not an outside finding. Watch Interpol's handling of Russian requests and the funding of foreign media outlets.

San Marino.imp: Nothing on the map shows hidden control in San Marino. Its closeness to Italy's banking and lodge networks is the thing to watch.

Serbia.d: On 11 June 1903 Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis' and junior officers stormed the royal palace in Belgrade and killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga, bringing the Karađorđević dynasty to the throne. In 1911 Dimitrijević and fellow officers founded the secret society Unification or Death (the Black Hand), which Britannica describes as dominating the army and pressuring the government, and in 1913 he became chief of intelligence of the Serbian General Staff; many scholars hold that he sanctioned the 1914 Sarajevo assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. In 1917 Prince Regent Alexander had him court-martialled at Salonika for treason, he and two others were shot and more than 200 members imprisoned, but in 1953 the Supreme Court of Serbia acquitted them for lack of proof of the plot against the Prince Regent. The rival White Hand, founded in 1912 by officers led by Petar Živković, gained influence over Alexander after the Salonika trial, and when he suspended the constitution on 6 January 1929 with White Hand support, Živković became Prime Minister until 1932. Serbia is a case in the pattern of sworn brotherhoods that ran the government, and in the exposure-and-reversal pattern through the 1953 annulment of the Salonika verdict.
Serbia.imp: For about 30 years, secret societies of army officers killed one king, ran military intelligence and later installed a prime minister under a royal dictatorship. The one court verdict against the Black Hand's leader was overturned decades later for lack of proof. Watch for officers' networks inside the army and intelligence services that answer to their own leaders rather than to elected government.

Slovakia.imp: The map does not document hidden control in Slovakia, but its weaker resilience score means influence would be harder to see. Funding of parties and media by outside states is the thing to watch.

Spain.d: In February 1957 Franco appointed two Opus Dei members to his cabinet: Mariano Navarro Rubio as finance minister and Alberto Ullastres as trade minister; both served until 1965 and drove the Stabilisation Plan that ended autarky, and historians count 8 Opus Dei members among Franco's 116 ministers, none before 1957. Laureano López Rodó, an Opus Dei member close to Luis Carrero Blanco, ran development planning from 1962 and was minister for it from 1965 to 1973, and Gregorio López-Bravo was industry minister and then foreign minister from 1969 to 1973; Navarro Rubio went on to govern the Bank of Spain from 1965. The MATESA scandal broke on 23 July 1969 over about 10 billion pesetas in export credits from the state industrial bank; Navarro Rubio and two other former ministers were charged, and Franco pardoned them before any verdict. The reshuffle of 29 October 1969 then produced a 'monocolor' cabinet in which eleven members had ties to Opus Dei. After Italy's 1990 disclosure, Defence Minister Narcís Serra opened an inquiry into a Spanish stay-behind network; former prime minister Leopoldo Calvo Sotelo said the Franco regime 'itself was Gladio'. Spain is the main European case in the pattern of faith movements placing members in the state and a documented case in the anticommunist web; in the private-forums pattern WEF lists José María Aznar, Prime Minister in 1996–2004, among its 1993 Global Leaders for Tomorrow, a selection no forum has found directed his decisions.
Spain.imp: Under Franco, members of one religious organisation held the economy, trade, planning and foreign ministries and the central bank, and in 1969 eleven cabinet members had ties to it. When a credit scandal reached three former ministers, the dictator pardoned them before any court ruled. Watch whether members of organised religious movements in high office state those ties.

Sweden.d: On 3 May 1973 journalists Jan Guillou and Peter Bratt revealed in Folket i Bild/Kulturfront that IB, a secret military intelligence bureau with no official status, monitored and registered people with far-left views and infiltrated left-wing groups, including break-ins at the Communist Party's offices. Former security chief P.G. Vinge wrote that IB director Birger Elmér had regular contact with Prime Minister Olof Palme and reported to Social Democratic party secretary Sven Andersson; Palme denied any link. The journalists, not IB staff, were convicted of espionage on 4 January 1974. A 2002 public inquiry report, 'Rikets säkerhet och den personliga integriteten', set out IB's operations. Sweden is a documented case in the anticommunist web of 1945–1990 and an example of exposure followed by inquiry.
Sweden.imp: A bureau without legal status spied on citizens for their political views and, by one former security chief's account, reported to the governing party's secretary. The people punished were the journalists who revealed it, and the full account came out in an official report almost 30 years later. Watch whether intelligence work is kept separate from party politics and whether those who expose it are protected.

Switzerland.d: A parliamentary commission of inquiry into the Defence Department (PUK EMD) reported in November 1990 that a secret cadre organisation, P-26, existed outside parliamentary and government control; led from 1979 by Colonel Efrem Cattelan, it had up to about 1,000 members in about 40 regions and cost about 54.3 million francs of federal money, and it was dissolved that month. Judge Pierre Cornu's report found that P-26 lacked political or legal legitimacy and that its cooperation with British intelligence was extensive, but only a 17-page summary titled 'P-26 not part of an international network' was published in 1991, and the full report is sealed until 2041. In 2000 a WHO expert committee chaired by Thomas Zeltner found an 'elaborate, well financed, sophisticated and usually invisible' tobacco-industry effort to undermine WHO tobacco control, which led into the 2003 Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. In 2010 the Council of Europe's Parliamentary Assembly voted 60-1 that the H1N1 response wasted public money and had 'grave shortcomings' in transparency that raised concerns about drug-industry influence, while not finding proven industry control. Switzerland is a documented case in the anticommunist web, a site of exposure by parliament, the host of WHO in the pattern of governments and industries inside international bodies, and the headquarters of the World Economic Forum in the private-forums pattern.
Switzerland.imp: A secret organisation run with federal money and tied to British intelligence existed outside the control of parliament and government, and the full findings are still sealed. Separately, an inquiry found the tobacco industry working out of sight inside a UN health agency based in Geneva. Watch whether the Cornu report is released and how international bodies in Switzerland disclose who advises them.

As a best-judgement estimate, the most likely source of outside reach is Russian state networks, including the Voice of Europe network run by Viktor Medvedchuk that the Czech government sanctioned in 2024, alongside networks already embedded in state bodies.
Ukraine.imp: The map does not document hidden control inside Ukraine's government. The scores and the Voice of Europe case point to foreign-state money and officials with outside ties as the things to watch.

United Kingdom.d: Carroll Quigley, citing Lord Esher's journals, says Esher was named in 1891 with W. T. Stead and Alfred Milner to the 'Junta of Three' of Cecil Rhodes's secret society; Esher then chaired the 1904 War Office reform committee that created the Army Council. Milner sat in Lloyd George's War Cabinet from December 1916 to November 1918 and then served as War and Colonial Secretary, and Philip Kerr, founding editor of The Round Table, was the Prime Minister's private secretary from 1916 to 1921, a placement historian John Turner examined in 1977 and found Milner's influence on its staffing. Geoffrey Dawson, Milner's former secretary, edited The Times in 1912–19 and 1923–41 and wrote in 1937 that he took out anything that might hurt German susceptibilities; Quigley also counts Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax, who defended the Munich Agreement in 1938, in the group's inner core, a membership claim that is his. Chatham House grew from a meeting Lionel Curtis convened in Paris in 1919, and its wartime research service was moved into the Foreign Office from 1943 to 1946. From 1978 Operation Countryman investigated corruption among London detectives, with allegations later raised of ties to particular Masonic lodges; eight officers were prosecuted and none convicted, and DCI Brian Woollard told Parliament in 1985 that he had been taken off an Islington fraud inquiry when it pointed to Freemasonry. In 1997 the Commons Home Affairs Committee recommended that police, judges, magistrates and prosecutors register membership of secret societies; from 1998 new appointees had to declare, but Justice Secretary Jack Straw ended the rule for judges in 2009 after a review found no impropriety, and in 2021 the Daniel Morgan Panel found no corrupt use of Masonic channels in that case but recommended confidential disclosure. In February 2026 the High Court upheld the Metropolitan Police's new rule making Freemasonry declarable, by which time 397 officers and staff had declared. On 13 January 2022 MI5 warned MPs that solicitor Christine Lee had acted covertly with the Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department; she had donated to Barry Gardiner MP, whose office employed her son, and the Investigatory Powers Tribunal upheld the alert in 2024, and in 2023 the Home Secretary excluded Yang Tengbo, a guest of Prince Andrew at royal residences, an exclusion upheld in 2024 though judges found 'not an abundance of evidence' of United Front links. Le Cercle was chaired in the UK by sitting MPs including Rory Stewart (2013–14) and Nadhim Zahawi (2015–18), who, PoliticsHome reported, sat on the Foreign Affairs Committee and did not declare the chairmanship. The UK is the London centre of the Rhodes–Milner–Round Table network, the target country for United Front activity, a documented case of lodges inside police and courts, and a booking centre in the hidden-money pattern through BCCI's Leadenhall Street headquarters; in the private-forums pattern it lists Geoffrey Howe (Mont Pelerin), Tony Blair and Gordon Brown (WEF 1993) and David Cameron (WEF Young Global Leaders), none found to have been directed by those bodies, and in the faith pattern Education Secretary Ruth Kelly, who said in 2005 she received spiritual support from Opus Dei.
United Kingdom.imp: Early in the 20th century, men from one circle around Milner held a War Cabinet seat, ran the Prime Minister's private office and edited the main national newspaper, though the claim that they acted as a single secret group rests largely on Quigley. Later, Parliament spent years trying to find out how many police and judges were Masons, and the Grand Lodge produced a list for one disbanded police squad only after five attempts; inquiries have not found Masonic channels used corruptly in the cases examined. The recent alerts concern a foreign party's agents reaching MPs and the royal family. Watch disclosure rules for police and judges, and declarations by MPs of their roles in private foreign-policy clubs.

Vatican City.d: The Vatican Bank (IOR) was Banco Ambrosiano's main shareholder and was tied to the offshore companies that held the roughly US$1.287 billion missing when it collapsed in 1982; in 1984 the IOR denied legal liability but acknowledged 'moral involvement' and paid US$224 million to about 120 creditor banks. In February 1987 Milan magistrates issued arrest warrants for IOR president Archbishop Paul Marcinkus and officials Luigi Mennini and Pellegrino de Strobel as accessories to the bank's fraudulent bankruptcy, but on 17 July 1987 Italy's Court of Cassation held that the 1929 Lateran Treaty shielded the IOR's central bodies; Marcinkus stayed inside Vatican City and was never tried. On 21 January 2021 the Vatican tribunal convicted former IOR president Angelo Caloia and lawyer Gabriele Liuzzo of embezzlement and self-laundering over IOR property sales in 2002–2007, sentencing each to eight years and eleven months and ordering forfeiture of about €38 million. In July 2016 Monsignor Lucio Vallejo Balda, a senior official of the economic prefecture, was sentenced to 18 months for leaking confidential documents. Cardinal Angelo Becciu, Substitute at the Secretariat of State from 2011 to 2018, was convicted in December 2023 over a €350 million London property investment, but on 17 March 2026 the appeals tribunal nullified the indictment over unpublished papal decrees and undisclosed evidence and ordered a retrial. The Vatican is the bank headquarters in the pattern of banks that carried the hidden money, linked through Ambrosiano to the P2 cases in Italy, and an example of a court reversing a finding in the Becciu case. Its conditions scores are Italy's, as the Global Organized Crime Index does not score the Holy See.
Vatican City.imp: The Vatican's bank stood behind the shell companies at the centre of the Ambrosiano collapse, and a treaty kept its president beyond the reach of Italian courts. Later cases show the Vatican's own tribunal convicting a former bank president, while its most senior conviction, of Cardinal Becciu, has been annulled pending retrial. Watch the Becciu retrial and whether the Holy See's finances are opened to outside audit.

Argentina.d: The Italian lodge Propaganda Due (P2) had members at the top of Argentina's government in the 1970s. The P2 lists seized from Licio Gelli's files in March 1981, and studied by Italy's Anselmi Commission, include interim president Raúl Lastiri (1973), foreign minister Alberto Vignes, economy minister Celestino Rodrigo, joint chiefs head Luis Betti, navy commander and junta member Emilio Massera, General Carlos Guillermo Suárez Mason, later head of the state oil company YPF, and social welfare minister José López Rega, whose ministry funded the Triple A death squad blamed for about 1,500 deaths. In August 1974 a decree drafted by Perón and Vignes gave Gelli a state honour and a post at Argentina's embassy in Italy; he later held four Argentine diplomatic passports and advised Isabel Perón and López Rega on money. Massera was sentenced to life in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas and Suárez Mason was convicted of 43 murders, but President Menem pardoned both in 1990. Suárez Mason also chaired the Latin American chapter of the World Anti-Communist League, which, with the 2016 Operation Condor verdict convicting 15 officers including ex-dictator Reynaldo Bignone, makes Argentina a documented case in the anticommunist web. In the banks pattern, a 1992 indictment of BCCI cited a $500,000 'political' payment to central bank officials in 1983–84; later threads include P2-listed diplomat Federico Barttfeld, removed as under-secretary in 2003, and Atlas Network think tank Fundación Pensar, which merged into Mauricio Macri's PRO party in 2015.
Argentina.imp: For most of the 1970s, members of a private Italian lodge sat at the head of the state, the cabinet, the navy and the army, and its grand master carried Argentine diplomatic passports; the public learned this only when Italian police found the lists in 1981. Some of these men were later convicted for the repression, but pardons undid much of that. Watch for honours, diplomatic posts or advisory roles handed to foreign private figures, and pardons that end cases before the full record is public.

Bahamas.d: The one documented case is a bank. Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau was a subsidiary of Roberto Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano, and Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, president of the Vatican Bank (IOR), had been one of its directors. After Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982, Bahamian banking authorities suspended the Nassau unit. The Nassau and Luxembourg units owed about half of the $1.2–1.4 billion lent to Panamanian shell companies, the same lending that ran through Ambrosiano's banks in Lima and Managua. In the pattern 'Banks that carried the hidden money' the Bahamas served as a booking centre, and in 'Exposure, purge and reversal' it is a case where the government shut the operation down. BCCI's presence is considered likely but is not documented here.
Bahamas.imp: The Bahamas was a place where money was booked, not where officials were captured: a Vatican Bank chief sat on a Nassau board while large loans went to shell companies. The regulator acted only after the collapse. Watch offshore units whose real owners and directors the public cannot easily see.

Bolivia.d: Both documented cases centre on General Luis García Meza's coup of 17 July 1980, which Argentina's junta backed. Journalist Robert Parry wrote in 1998 that the Unification Church published a photo of Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak meeting García Meza after the coup, quoting Pak: 'I have erected a throne for Father Moon in the world's highest city.' Parry also wrote, without naming a source, that Moon's group CAUSA ran joint operations with the junta and that later Bolivian investigations found it had put about US$4 million into the coup; this is a single-author account. Luis Arce Gómez, García Meza's interior minister and chief of repression, received a life sentence from a Rome appeals court in July 2019 in the Operation Condor case, a verdict still open to appeal at Italy's top court. Bolivia is a documented case in the anticommunist web and, through the Bo Hi Pak link (Pak also appears in Uruguay in 1981 and as founding president of The Washington Times), in the pattern of faith movements placing members near government.
Bolivia.imp: The record describes a government that took power by force with help from Argentina's junta and, by one journalist's account, money from the Unification Church network. The Moon part has not been tested in any court; the only conviction came from Italy 39 years later. Watch for foreign religious or political groups offering money or publicity to governments that come to power outside elections.

Brazil.d: In the October 1962 elections the Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action (IBAD), linked to the CIA and backed by multinational companies, paid for many opposition campaigns for Congress and eleven state governments; a parliamentary inquiry investigated, President Goulart closed IBAD in 1963, and in 1977 former US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted the US had funded the opposition. Historians say the Brazil-founded group Tradition, Family, Property (TFP), by campaigning against Goulart's land reform, helped set the stage for the 1964 coup, and AIFLD director William Doherty Jr. said his institute's Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in it, though historian Cliff Welch says what they did 'remains unclear'. The US Senate BCCI report (1992) found BCCI secretly controlled a Brazilian bank through nominees, including close associates of President José Sarney, and that Sarney presented a BCCI-funded prize in 1987. In 2014 federal prosecutors released colonel Paulo Malhães's papers on 'Operation Gringo', which Attorney-General Rodrigo Janot called the strongest evidence that Operation Condor existed; the armed forces deny the collaboration. In sport, ex-São Paulo governor José Maria Marin was convicted in New York in 2017 of taking football bribes, Rio governor Sérgio Cabral testified in 2019 that he paid $2 million to IOC member Lamine Diack for votes for Rio's 2009 Olympic bid, and Olympic chief Carlos Nuzman was sentenced in 2021 to 30 years, 11 months over the same payment, while free on appeal. Brazil is where intelligence money went (IBAD, AIFLD), a documented case in the anticommunist web and the banks pattern, and a case of officials inside international bodies.
Brazil.imp: Before 1964, money from a foreign government and companies paid for Brazilian election campaigns through a local institute, and voters learned whose money it was only through an inquiry and, years later, a US ambassador's admission. Later the routes were a bank fronted by nominees close to a president, and sports bodies where a former governor and Olympic officials took or paid bribes. Watch campaign money from institutes with unnamed donors, and the bidding for major international events.

Canada.d: Sworn brotherhoods held real power in Canada for long stretches. Four prime ministers were Orangemen, including Mackenzie Bowell (1894–96), a past Grand Master; every Toronto mayor in the first half of the 20th century belonged to the Orange Order, and in 1942 16 of 23 council members did, a run that ended in 1954. Its French Catholic rival, the Ordre de Jacques-Cartier ('La Patente', founded 1926), recruited figures such as Montreal mayor Jean Drapeau and Pierre Laporte and steered francophones into federal public service jobs, peaking at 11,300 members before an insider exposed it in 1964 and it dissolved in 1965; in Saskatchewan the Klan claimed 40,000 members before the 1929 election that ousted the Liberals, though no proof of a Klan–Conservative alliance exists. In the Rhodes, Milner and Round Table network Canada was a dominion group: Rhodes trustee Earl Grey was Governor General from 1904 to 1911 and Milner's Kindergarten member John Buchan from 1935 to 1940. The one court finding of planted insiders came in 1992, when the Church of Scientology of Toronto was convicted of breach of the public trust for placing members in the Ontario Provincial Police and the Attorney General's offices, and fined $250,000. As a target of other states' networks, Special Rapporteur David Johnston found in 2023 a 'well-grounded suspicion' that irregularities in Han Dong's 2019 nomination were tied to the PRC consulate in Toronto but no evidence Dong knew, and in 2025 the elections commissioner found no breach of election law; NSICOP reported in 2024 that unnamed parliamentarians were 'semi-witting or witting' participants in foreign interference, while the Hogue Commission found in January 2025 no evidence of 'traitors' in Parliament.
Canada.imp: For much of Canada's history, membership in the Orange Order or La Patente helped decide who ran city halls and filled public jobs, and citizens saw the results without seeing the membership lists. The only court finding of planted insiders is the 1992 Scientology case. The recent foreign-interference findings are suspicions about unnamed people, and later reviews cleared Han Dong of breaking election law; the things to watch are party nomination races and money passed through proxies of foreign missions.

Chile.d: Chile was the coordinating centre of Operation Condor: the DINA intelligence service under Manuel Contreras called the founding meeting in Santiago in November 1975. DINA agents killed former foreign minister Orlando Letelier with a car bomb in Washington in September 1976, and in 1995 Chile's Supreme Court upheld the convictions of Contreras (seven years) and his deputy Pedro Espinoza; Judge Juan Guzmán indicted Pinochet for Condor crimes in 2004, but he died in 2006 unconvicted. The Rettig truth commission (1991) found DINA held prisoners at Colonia Dignidad, a German sect compound near Parral, where some residents helped torture them. Chile's economy was run by graduates of a US-funded programme linking the University of Chicago with the Catholic University: 126 Chileans trained there in 1955–73, their plan 'El ladrillo' became the junta's economic programme in 1975, and graduates held top posts, among them Sergio de Castro (economy, then finance, 1975–82) and Miguel Kast (planning, labour, then Central Bank governor in 1982). The group Tradition, Family, Property was banned by Eduardo Frei's government in the late 1960s and later disowned by Chile's bishops. After 2010, Opus Dei member Joaquín Lavín was education then social development minister under Piñera, and Cristián Larroulet, director of the Atlas Network partner Libertad y Desarrollo, became Minister Secretary-General of the Presidency; both are lawful memberships. Salvador Allende was a Freemason, but no lodge direction of his government is documented.
Chile.imp: The military government ran a cross-border repression network from Santiago and handed its economy to economists trained under a foreign-funded programme, so the plans behind both were made outside public view. Courts later convicted the intelligence chief, but Pinochet died without a verdict. Since 2010 the links are lawful ones, such as movement members and think-tank directors in the cabinet; the thing to watch is whether a think tank's programme becomes government policy without public debate.

Guatemala.d: Mario Sandoval Alarcón, who founded the National Liberation Movement (MLN) in 1960, was vice-president of Guatemala from 1974 to 1978 while a leader of the World Anti-Communist League; historians link the MLN to killings by the Mano Blanca death squad. That places Guatemala as a documented case in the anticommunist web. The second case comes through football: Héctor Trujillo, a sitting judge listed as on the Constitutional Court and general secretary of the national football federation, was arrested in December 2015 when his cruise ship docked in Florida, charged in the US FIFA case with taking bribes for World Cup qualifier marketing rights, pleaded guilty and was jailed. He is Guatemala's entry in the pattern of officials inside international bodies, alongside Honduras's former president Rafael Callejas in the same US case.
Guatemala.imp: A vice-president in the 1970s was also a leader of an international anticommunist league tied, through his party, to a death squad. Four decades later a senior judge was taking bribes as a football official. Watch officials who hold a second post in a private or international body, where the money and loyalties are hard for the public to see.

Honduras.d: In the early 1980s the armed forces commander, General Gustavo Álvarez Martínez, headed the Association for the Progress of Honduras (APROH), which joined officers and business leaders; a Library of Congress country study says it received US$50,000 from a front group for the Unification Church. The Christian Science Monitor reported in March 1984 that APROH and allied forces had taken control of university, professional, teacher, labour and peasant bodies. Fellow officers ousted Álvarez on 31 March 1984 and APROH declined. Rafael Callejas, president from 1990 to 1994, later headed the Honduran football federation; indicted in the US FIFA case in December 2015, he pleaded guilty in March 2016 to taking $500,000 in bribes in 2012, and FIFA banned him for life. Honduras appears in the pattern of faith movements placing members near government through APROH, and in the pattern of officials inside international bodies through Callejas. World Anti-Communist League presence is considered likely but is not documented.
Honduras.imp: The head of the army ran a private association, part-funded by a Moon group front, that took over civic bodies until his own officers removed him. A former president later admitted taking bribes as a football chief. Watch private associations led by serving military officers, and former leaders who move into bodies that handle large contracts.

Jamaica.d: Under Prime Minister Edward Seaga, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) handled Jamaica's US commodity financing and most of the government's foreign-currency accounts. A BCCI officer told the US Senate: 'we handled every penny that came into or out of Jamaica in terms of foreign currency.' The Senate's 1992 report lists BCCI loans of $33.9 million to the Bank of Jamaica and $45.4 million to the state oil firm Petrojam. Jamaica is a documented case in the pattern 'Banks that carried the hidden money', and was exposed through the same Senate inquiry that found BCCI secretly owned First American Bank in Washington and that the CIA kept using it after knowing it was a criminal enterprise.
Jamaica.imp: A single foreign bank, later found by a US Senate inquiry to be criminal, held nearly all of a government's foreign currency, which gave it a close view of and leverage over the state's finances. Jamaicans did not see this until a foreign legislature reported it. Watch how much of a country's reserves and state-company borrowing sits with one private bank.

Mexico.d: All three Mexican cases concern El Yunque, a secret Catholic group founded in Puebla in 1953, and all rest on reporting and allegations that the people named denied. In 2003 journalist Álvaro Delgado's book claimed El Yunque had members among PAN party leaders and in President Vicente Fox's cabinet; PAN officials called it 'pure fiction', and former PAN leader Luis H. Álvarez said he thought the group was real but negligible. In the 2000s Guanajuato governor Juan Manuel Oliva, his chief of staff Gerardo Mosqueda and politician Alberto Diosdado were named as members, and all three denied it. In 2007 former Puebla mayor Luis Paredes Moctezuma named PAN national leader Manuel Espino as a member, said the group helped Fox's 2000 campaign, and claimed it controlled four state governments; the PAN denied any tie. These cases place Mexico in the pattern of faith movements placing members in government. Mexico is also headquarters of the Legion of Christ, and Opus Dei, NXIVM, the World Anti-Communist League and the Congress for Cultural Freedom have documented presence without cases on this map.
Mexico.imp: If the claims are true, a secret religious group had members inside the governing party and some state governments, and voters could not tell who answered to it. No court or inquiry has confirmed any of it, and everyone named denied it. Watch for clusters of appointees from one closed network, and for parties that refuse to answer plain questions about members' outside loyalties.

Nicaragua.d: Ambrosiano Group Banco Comercial, a unit of Roberto Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano Holding, was licensed in Nicaragua in 1977–78 and gave funds to both the Somoza government and the Sandinista opposition. On 2 August 1985 Daniel Ortega signed Presidential Agreement No. 39, moving the bank's seat out of the country and cancelling its licence. That places Nicaragua in the banks pattern as a booking centre, in the anticommunist web, and in 'Exposure, purge and reversal' as a government that shut the operation. Historian William LeoGrande writes that the National Endowment for Democracy (NED) gave about $2 million in 1984–88, the main open aid to the civic opposition, about half to La Prensa, the paper run by Violeta Chamorro; in October 1989 the US House voted 263–156 for a further $9 million before the 25 February 1990 election, which Chamorro's coalition won. Critics compared this to earlier CIA operations in Chile; NED says its grants are public and nonpartisan, and its founder said in 1991 that much of its work 'was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA'. In the pattern of intelligence money behind international NGOs, Nicaragua is where the money went.
Nicaragua.imp: An Italian bank played both sides of a civil conflict before the new government expelled it. A decade later a foreign government openly funded the opposition newspaper and coalition that won the next election. Watch how much of an election's opposition funding comes from abroad, and whether voters are told.

Panama.d: Both Panamanian cases come from the US Senate's 1992 BCCI report. General Manuel Noriega opened a BCCI account in early 1982 in the name of the Panamanian Defense Forces; it held about $25 million at its height, mostly cash, with one deposit of about $4 million, and BCCI absorbed about $10 million in losses on loans to Noriega associates Enrique Pretelt and César Rodríguez. The report also found that Noriega had BCCI pay off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta, his chosen presidential candidate, who became president in 1984. Panama's BCCI branch also held Peru's central bank reserves, $270 million by June 1987, and Panamanian shell companies received the $1.2–1.4 billion lent by Banco Ambrosiano. Panama is a documented case in 'Banks that carried the hidden money' and, through the Senate inquiry, in 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Panama.imp: The commander of the armed forces kept tens of millions in cash at a foreign bank under his army's name and used the same bank to help the man he made president. Panamanians did not see this until a US Senate committee reported it. Watch for officials' personal debts paid by banks or firms that want something from the state.

Paraguay.d: On 22 December 1992 lawyer Martín Almada and judge José Agustín Fernández found the records of Alfredo Stroessner's secret police in a police station in Lambaré; the 'Archives of Terror' proved Operation Condor existed and include Chilean intelligence chief Manuel Contreras's invitation to the 25 November 1975 meeting in Santiago where it was founded. Paraguay's Truth and Justice Commission used them to document 9,923 people who suffered 14,338 violations. The US Senate BCCI report lists a $5 million deposit by Paraguay's Central Bank at BCCI on 10 October 1989, and says BCCI's Paraguay ties came through Saudi businessman Ghaith Pharaon's friendship with Stroessner; Pharaon is the same man whose BCCI-linked purchase of a California bank the FDIC approved in 1985. In 2000 Moon's representatives bought about 600,000 hectares in the north, including the town of Puerto Casado, and in August 2005 the Senate voted 24–14 to expropriate 52,000 hectares for its roughly 6,000 residents. Paraguay is a documented case in the anticommunist web and the banks pattern, and appears in the faith-movement pattern through the Moon land dispute.
Paraguay.imp: Under Stroessner the secret police shared files with neighbouring dictatorships, and the central bank's dealings with BCCI ran through a dictator's personal friendship; both came to light only after the regime fell. The Moon land purchase put a whole town on private land owned by a religious movement. Watch personal ties between rulers and foreign financiers, and large land sales that include the homes of residents.

Peru.d: During the 1982 Falklands war, British intelligence found that the guarantee for Exocet missiles Peru was buying, which France then blocked to keep them from Argentina, was a $200 million deposit from Banco Ambrosiano Andino in Lima, a subsidiary of Calvi's bank whose Latin American units lent to Panamanian shell companies the Vatican Bank described as under its control. Peru's Central Reserve Bank placed reserves at BCCI-Panama, reaching $270 million in June 1987, about three-tenths of the government's cash reserves; a 1991 New York indictment alleged $3 million in bribes for the deposits, Peruvian reporting named former central bank president Leonel Figueroa and general manager Héctor Neyra, who denied it, and a congressional commission led by Fernando Olivera alleged President Alan García was the real beneficiary, which García called a fabrication. Opus Dei priest Juan Luis Cipriani was named by President Fujimori as a mediator in the 1996–97 Japanese embassy hostage crisis; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission later said that as bishop of Ayacucho he never questioned abuses by state forces, a finding he rejected. Opus Dei numerary Rafael Rey was minister of production (2006–08) and defence (2009–10) under the same Alan García. In July 2019 a Rome appeals court gave former de facto president Francisco Morales Bermúdez a life sentence in absentia in the Operation Condor case, subject to appeal. Peru is a documented case in the anticommunist web, a booking centre in the banks pattern, and appears in the faith-movement pattern through Cipriani and Rey.
Peru.imp: Peru's central bank put close to a third of its cash reserves in one foreign bank, and an inquiry alleged the decision was bought; the people named denied it and no Peruvian court is recorded as ruling on it. An Italian bank's Lima unit guaranteed a wartime arms deal outside public view. Watch where central bank reserves are held and who decides, and appointments of movement members to security posts.

Trinidad and Tobago.d: Jack Warner was FIFA vice-president and president of CONCACAF, the regional football body, until 2011, and from 2010 sat in Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar's cabinet, first as Minister of Works and Transport and then as Minister of National Security. A CONCACAF Integrity Committee report of 18 April 2013 concluded he had committed fraud against CONCACAF and FIFA, and he resigned from the cabinet on 21 April 2013. US prosecutors indicted him in May 2015 for wire fraud, racketeering and money laundering, including a $10 million payment tied to South Africa's 2010 World Cup bid, and FIFA banned him for life. On 23 September 2025 Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition. Trinidad and Tobago is a documented case in the pattern of governments and officials inside international bodies, alongside officials from Brazil, Guatemala and Honduras in the same US case.
Trinidad and Tobago.imp: A man later found by his own sports body to have committed fraud was, at the same time, the minister in charge of national security. The case has not been tried, because the local court refused extradition. Watch ministers who keep senior posts in international bodies that handle large sums.

United States.d: Secret brotherhoods reached into American offices early: in the 1827 Morgan affair a Masonic sheriff, Eli Bruce, was convicted for his part in abducting a former Mason; the Know Nothings' secret order won the Massachusetts governorship and all 40 state Senate seats in 1854; and Tammany Society Grand Sachem William Tweed, who controlled New York City government, was convicted in 1873 on 204 of 220 counts. The 1920s Klan helped elect governors in Oregon (1922), Colorado (1924) and Indiana (1924, where Governor Ed Jackson was tried in 1928 for a Klan bribe offer and freed by a hung jury), and Denver's Klansman mayor Benjamin Stapleton appointed a Klansman police chief; in Alabama, Hugo Black, a Mason and Klan member, visited all 148 klaverns while winning his 1926 Senate primary and admitted the membership in 1937 after being confirmed to the Supreme Court. Later police cases include Klan ties found in the Fruitland Park, Florida, force in 2014 and a 2006 FBI warning about white supremacist 'ghost skins' seeking police jobs. In Scientology's Operation Snow White, the church's Guardian's Office planted Gerald Wolfe as an IRS clerk around 1974 and took documents from the Justice Department and a federal prosecutor's office; eleven Scientologists, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted in 1979, and in 1993 the IRS granted the church tax exemption under a secret agreement in which it paid $12.5 million. In Koreagate, Tongsun Park, acting for the Korean Central Intelligence Agency, admitted giving money to 30 members of Congress; Rep. Richard Hanna pleaded guilty, three congressmen were reprimanded in 1978 and Rep. Otto Passman was acquitted, while the Fraser Report found Sun Myung Moon's organisation had at times acted 'in cooperation with, or at the direction of' South Korean agencies and tried to buy a Washington bank with disguised funds; Moon was convicted of tax fraud in 1982, the year he founded The Washington Times with Bo Hi Pak as president. The Senate's 1992 BCCI report found the bank secretly controlled First American, Washington's largest bank, after the Federal Reserve approved the takeover on false assurances, that it paid off Bert Lance's debts in 1977, and that the CIA kept using it after knowing it was criminal; chairman Clark Clifford, a former Defense Secretary, was indicted in 1992 (charges dropped for ill health) and his partner Robert Altman was acquitted. As the American counterpart in the Round Table network, the Council on Foreign Relations, which Carroll Quigley described as a front for J. P. Morgan and Company with the American Round Table Group, sent 682 confidential memoranda to the State Department in 1939–45 under a programme led in part by future CIA director Allen Dulles, and a 1977 study found more than half of 502 senior officials in 1945–72 were members; Carter, Mondale, Brzezinski, Vance, Brown and 17 others in the Carter administration came from the Trilateral Commission, memberships that are lawful and documented rather than found to be misconduct. As the funding centre for intelligence money behind private groups, the CIA set up the Asia Foundation as a proprietary, paid for the National Student Association's international work until Ramparts exposed it in 1967, and, by the Church Committee's 1976 count, was behind at least 108 of 700 large grants by 164 foundations in 1963–66, before the National Endowment for Democracy took on part of this work openly from 1983. As a target of another state's networks, prosecutors charged Linda Sun, a deputy chief of staff to New York's governor, as a PRC agent in 2024 (mistrial in December 2025, retrial planned), and Arcadia, California, campaign treasurer Mike Sun and Mayor Eileen Wang pleaded guilty in 2025 and 2026 to acting for China; a 2020 report on Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese operative who placed an intern with a congressman, led to no charges.
United States.imp: The US record runs in two directions. At home, closed groups reached sheriffs' offices, governors' mansions, the Supreme Court and the IRS, and foreign governments paid or placed people close to lawmakers, from South Korea in the 1970s to China in the 2020s; the proven cases are the court and congressional findings above, while much about elite clubs and councils is documented membership, not proven direction. Abroad, the US government itself funded private-looking groups through the CIA, and later openly through NED. Watch campaign treasurers and staff with foreign contacts, bank ownership hidden behind nominees, and foundations or nonprofits that do not say where their money comes from.

Uruguay.d: After Italy issued an arrest warrant on 22 May 1981, P2 grand master Licio Gelli took refuge in Uruguay, where police seized files at his Montevideo villa, reportedly on a CIA tip; an Italian military intelligence mission later found only about 300 files left and recovered about 70 incomplete ones. The same year Moon's group bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of Uruguay's oldest banks, and founded the daily Últimas Noticias, whose early editorial declared it 'fully identified' with the military 'process', and Moon aide Bo Hi Pak, who appears in Bolivia's 1980 coup, met de facto president Aparicio Méndez, according to a book by Juan de Montemayor. When Banco de Crédito closed in 2002, a parliamentary commission found it had lent about US$100 million of its roughly US$600 million in loans to Moon-linked companies. Former army commander and last de facto president Gregorio Álvarez was sentenced in 2009 to 25 years for 37 homicides, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2011, with several victims moved to Argentina in 1978 under the Condor plan; former foreign minister Juan Carlos Blanco received a life sentence from a Rome appeals court in 2019, subject to appeal. Uruguay is a documented case in the anticommunist web, and the Moon bank case places it in the faith-movement pattern and in 'Exposure, purge and reversal'.
Uruguay.imp: During the dictatorship a foreign religious movement bought into a major bank and a newspaper that backed the generals, and a sixth of the bank's lending ended up with that movement's companies; the public learned the scale only when the bank failed and parliament looked into it. Courts at home and abroad later convicted top officials for the repression. Watch foreign groups buying banks and media under governments that face no elections.

Venezuela.d: In 1984, after parents complained that Tradition, Family, Property (TFP) cut teenagers off from their families, a three-month government investigation under President Jaime Lusinchi found the group was operating outside the constitution, and a ban was reported to be planned; whether it took effect is not confirmed. That December, Caracas police arrested a man carrying a TFP card over a possible plot against Pope John Paul II, and TFP denied involvement. Cedice Libertad, the Atlas Network's main think tank in Caracas, received regular grants from 1998 from the Center for International Private Enterprise, an NED core institute, and one grant letter lists NED funds for Cedice to advocate 'a change in government'. Cedice's director was among the signers of the 'Carmona Decree', which dissolved the National Assembly and Supreme Court during the April 2002 coup against Hugo Chávez. Venezuela appears in the faith-movement pattern through the TFP inquiry, and in the pattern of private forums placing members in office through Cedice; its state-embedded actors score is very high (9.0 of 10) and its resilience very low (1.9).
Venezuela.imp: A think tank funded in part by a US government-backed endowment had its director sign the decree of a coup government that shut down parliament and the courts. Venezuelans could see the decree but not the funding behind the people who signed it. Watch foreign grants whose stated aim is changing a government, and which think-tank figures appear in any emergency or transitional government.
